articles.title: La placa tectónica de Oceanía es la más rápida de la Tierra, desplazándose siete centímetros cada año, casi el doble de rápido de lo que crecen las uñas
articles.standfirst: El movimiento es imperceptible para quienes estén en su superficie
articles.summary: El movimiento es imperceptible para quienes estén en su superficie
articles.body: Australia se mueve. Y lo hace a un ritmo que, aunque imperceptible para cualquiera que esté sobre su superficie, resulta sorprendentemente rápido a escala geológica: unos siete centímetros cada año hacia el noreste. Es suficiente para convertirla en la masa continental que más rápido se desplaza sobre la Tierra. La cifra adquiere una dimensión más fácil de entender si se compara con algo cotidiano, con una acción a la que estamos totalmente acostumbrados. Un estudio calculó que las uñas crecen, de media, unos 3,47 milímetros al mes, alrededor de 4,2 centímetros al año. Es decir, Australia avanza aproximadamente 1,7 veces más rápido que una uña humana, apunta el medio de comunicación Science Blog. La velocidad tampoco significa que Australia sea la placa tectónica más rápida del planeta en términos absolutos. Existen zonas de placas oceánicas que superan los diez centímetros anuales. La particularidad australiana es que se trata de la masa continental que se desplaza más deprisa. Y ese movimiento tiene consecuencias prácticas. Australia ha tenido que actualizar sus sistemas de coordenadas porque el continente continúa desplazándose mientras los mapas permanecen estáticos. El antiguo sistema nacional de referencia fijaba las posiciones tomando como referencia la situación del territorio en 1994. Para 2020, la diferencia respecto a un marco global moderno había alcanzado aproximadamente 1,8 metros. La precisión es especialmente importante ahora que tecnologías como la agricultura de precisión, la topografía, la construcción o los sistemas de navegación trabajan con posicionamientos de centímetros. A una escala mucho mayor, el desplazamiento también está cambiando la posición de Australia respecto al resto del planeta. Durante millones de años se ha alejado de la Antártida y se ha acercado a la zona de Indonesia y Nueva Guinea. Algunos modelos geodinámicos incluso plantean que, dentro de 200 o 300 millones de años, Australia podría formar parte de un nuevo supercontinente. Pero esa última posibilidad es una predicción a una escala temporal enorme. Lo que sí sabemos es que Australia ya se está moviendo (siete centímetros cada año), y que la Tierra cambia mucho más de lo que aparentan sus mapas.

articles.title: Half-a-million 4K TV's to view one photo: Why Nasa's new space telescope is special
articles.summary: Science News: The story begins with an unexpected phone call. In Jan 2011, someone from the US’s highly secretive National Reconnaissance Office contacted a top Nas.
articles.body: The story begins with an unexpected phone call. In Jan 2011, someone from the US’s highly secretive National Reconnaissance Office contacted a top Nasa official about a couple of curved mirrors, two metres wide, their spy satellite programme no longer needed.The offer immediately excited Nasa brass for two main reasons: the mirrors were Hubble-size, and they were getting them for free.Over the next decade, a thousand engineers went to work, packing millions of delicate components around one of the mirrors. Their creation was ready by 2024. And it was launched last month, as one of the most advanced space telescopes ever built.The Nancy Grace Roman is on its way to an observation point 1.5 million kilometres away. Once there, it will power up a 300-megapixel camera, for some the largest panoramic shots of the Universe ever taken by a space telescope.It’s named after Nancy Grace Roman, Nasa's first chief of astronomy and its first woman executive, who in the early 1940s, was once asked why ‘a lady would prefer mathematics over Latin’. At Nasa, she was a strong advocate of space telescopes. Eight years after her demise at age 93, her namesake is set to revolutionise astronomy.Over its first five years of operations, Roman will survey 50 times the sky Hubble did in 30 years, beaming back 20 petabytes of data (roughly four billion songs), compared to Hubble’s 400Tb since 1990. During a single survey, lasting three weeks, this telescope, with a mirror donated by spies, will image an area equivalent to 3,455 full moons. To view the largest of these photos, one will theoretically need half-a-million 4K TVs — a screen size of nearly 250 acres, or the size of Delhi’s entire Red Fort complex.“We’re now in the golden age of astronomical data,” says Sangeeta Malhotra, a Nasa astrophysicist who’s been with the Roman programme since 2017. She was also part of the earliest scientific discussions, going as far back as 2005, that called for a wide-view tel-escope in space. Malhotra grew up in Karol Bagh in the 1980s, where she would wait for power cuts.“We slept on rooftops in the summers,” she says. “I would watch the sky pop with stars whenever the power went out.”She hung out with astronomers around the Nehru planetarium. And at 19, Malhotra ground a few mirrors, designed an assembly and made her first telescope. “I was an undergraduate studying physics at the time. I loved the theory and the maths, but amateur astronomy was the most fun we had. On the darkest nights, when lights were out, we would set up the telescope on the footpath, to give people a view of the Moon or Venus.”At 22, Malhotra left for the States and after a stint as a professor at Arizona State University, she joined Nasa, when she was “four Jupiter years” old. She’s with Roman’s science team, which works with engineers to execute research. She explains what sets apart this bus-sized space telescope from the two other famous ones — James Webb and Hubble.“Roman does this one thing very well,” Malhotra says, “which is survey large swaths of the sky. It has the light-gathering power and sharpness of Hubble, with 100 times its field of view. That is to say it images 100 times the patch of sky that Hubble or Webb would image during any pointing. It is also designed to survey the sky at 1,000 times Webb’s rate. Hubble and Webb are brilliant at detailed observations of specific objects. But they are less suitable for surveys.”Also aboard Roman is a coronagraph, designed to image exoplanets by cutting glare from host stars. A planet viewed without overwhelming starlight can throw up clues about its surface and even atmosphere. Roman’s coronagraph uses two mirrors whose surfaces can be adjusted in amounts smaller than the width of a DNA strand. It’s a tech demonstrator for future observatories, including Nasa’s proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory, which will look for a rock we could one day settle on.But the telescope Roman may work with quite perfectly is the Vera C Rubin Observatory on the ground in Chile, named after the woman whose groundbreaking research found the first clues to dark matter in galaxies.While Rubin will repeatedly photograph a much larger sky area in visible light, building a long time-lapse of changing stars and galaxies, Roman in space will see in near-infrared light through all the cosmic dust, separating objects that may blur or merge together in Rubin’s photos.Together, they offer one of our best shots at finding new planets, distant galaxies and massive black holes.“They were actually good friends, Vera Rubin and Nancy Grace Roman,” says Malhotra.“The two could be seen attending seminars together in the mid-2000s, asking hard questions. So it does seem fitting that data from telescopes named after them will one day be combined to give humanity the answers it seeks and the hard questions that must be asked.”

articles.title: In 2010, Thailand sank 25 retired battle tanks into the Gulf to rebuild fishing grounds; 9 years later, researchers found 53 fish species
articles.summary: Science News: Battle tank is made for war. It is built to cross tough terrain, take a beating and dominate a battlefield. But what if the battlefield disappears and.
articles.body: Battle tank is made for war. It is built to cross tough terrain, take a beating and dominate a battlefield. But what if the battlefield disappears and there is no place for the tank to go? Some retired tanks have found an unexpectedly useful second life, under the sea in southern Thailand. According to an online repor by Aljazeera, in August 2010 Thailand’s army sank 25 old Chinese-made battle tanks into the Gulf of Thailand off Narathiwat province. 273 old railroad cars and 198 scrapped garbage trucks went under the water to serve as an artificial reef and create new fishing grounds. The strange undersea haul was part of an effort to help fishing communities whose catches have plummeted after decades of overfishing. And then, over the next few years, something astonishing happened: the cast-off military hardware began to attract marine life.As per the report, it all began with a problem common to fishing communities around the world. Local fishermen in southern Thailand had complained of dwindling catches and finally appealed to Queen Sirikit for help. The response included an unusual thought, why not not just dump old equipment, but put it to work under the waves? The tanks were particularly well designed for the purpose, since they had already become obsolete. According to Bangkok Post reporting, Thailand bought them second-hand from China in 1987 at a discounted price and they were decommissioned in 2004. They were essentially steel not used by the army. But for the fishing industry, they could be something else entirely. The 2010 sinking, Al Jazeera reported, left the tanks next to hundreds of old railroad cars and scrapped garbage trucks. Collectively, the structures would supply the hard surfaces and shelter that a sandy seafloor cannot.What did they put in the tanks?Almost 10 years after the tanks went under, researchers from Ramkhamhaeng University in Bangkok did some diving to see what had grown up around the man-made reef sites. Their study “First Insight on the Fish Species Composition at Two Artificial Reef Areas, Narathiwat Province, Thailand” listed 53 fish species of 21 families that live around the tanks and the nearby sunken railroad wagons. Snappers were the most diverse group with seven species recorded. Then four species each of damselfish and wrasses. Also, the scientists found an interesting difference between the structures. The closed-in tanks held much larger schools of fish than the more open railroad wagons. Species recorded included commercially important fish such as snappers and the critically endangered humphead parrotfish. What had once been military hardware now offered shelter and feeding grounds and habitat for an underwater community.Why does a steel tank act like a reef?A reef does not necessarily have to look like coral to a fish. It’s the structure that’s important for what it provides. The flat, sandy seafloor provides relatively little for many reef-associated species. Vertical surfaces, crevices and sheltered spaces are created by a submerged tank, train car or other solid structure. As time goes by, algae, barnacles and other organisms colonize those surfaces. These tiny beasts then become food for smaller fish. The smaller fish attract bigger predators An abandoned piece of infrastructure can gradually become the basis for an entire food web. That is the simple idea behind artificial reefs. According to the report, this is not a practice unique to Thailand. Countries such as Japan, the United States and India have tried to create habitat and improve fishing grounds by using artificial structures built from boats, railroad materials, concrete and other durable materials.Figures suggest artificial reefs can pay offThe Narathiwat project seems to support local assertions that artificial reefs can improve fishing opportunities, but no independent study has quantified the increase in catches specifically around the Narathiwat tank reefs. But there is some interesting evidence elsewhere in the research. H. Mohamad Kasim and colleagues from India’s Central Marine Fisheries Research Institute published a study on the economic performance of artificial reefs along the Tamil Nadu coast in southern India in the Indian Journal of Fisheries in 2013. They found that fish catches per unit of fishing effort were 34% higher in reef areas compared to open fishing zones. Gillnet fisherman had a net income nearly three times greater near the artificial reefs. The scientists also discovered that the cost of building the reefs could be recouped in around two and a half months. But those results don't show that Thailand's tanks produced the same economic benefits. But they show why artificial reefs have become of interest as a tool to help fishing communities.Artificial reefs are not a magic bulletBut there is an important question behind the success stories. Are artificial reefs really increasing fish populations, or are they simply aggregating fish from elsewhere? The argument is not conclusively settled among scientists. An artificial reef that merely concentrates fish from a large area into a convenient location can look like a great success at first glance. Fishermen would catch more fish around the reef, but the overall population might not have grown. And that concentration could cause a new problem: overfishing. A popular artificial reef can be an easy target for fishermen and may deplete the very population it is intended to support. This is why successful artificial-reef programs often have fishing regulations such as catch limits or other restrictions to allow fish populations to reproduce. The performance of the reef can also depend on many environmental factors like depth, strength and direction of currents, materials used to build the reef and shape of the reef itself. Those variables might help explain why some artificial reefs become thriving ecosystems while others yield more modest results.A broader reef-building experimentThe tanks were not an isolated experiment. By 2008, Thailand's broader artificial-reef program in the region had already expanded to include donated railroad materials and concrete pipes supplied by government departments, including the state railway and highways authorities. The 2010 sinking of the tanks simply became its most striking and widely reported chapter. There is something almost poetic about the transformation. Objects designed to occupy battlefields were placed on the seabed and given an entirely different purpose.

articles.title: Scientists found an estimated 5.5 million wild bees beneath just 1.5 acres of a New York cemetery, more than three times Manhattan's human population
articles.summary: Wildlife & Biodiversity News: Beneath the quiet lawns and weathered headstones of a small cemetery in Ithaca, New York, scientists have uncovered one of the most astonishing bee di.
articles.body: Beneath the quiet lawns and weathered headstones of a small cemetery in Ithaca, New York, scientists have uncovered one of the most astonishing bee discoveries in recent memory. In a carefully studied 1.5-acre section of the cemetery grounds, researchers estimated that about 5.5 million wild, ground-nesting bees live in a dense network of underground nests. That number is more than three times the entire human population of Manhattan, packed into an area smaller than many city blocks. As reported by Cornell University and ScienceDaily, the finding highlights how urban and suburban landscapes can harbour vast, hidden reservoirs of biodiversity, and it challenges common assumptions about where nature thrives in a developed world.A cemetery that hums with lifeTo the casual visitor, the cemetery looks like many others in the Northeast. Grass is mowed in neat rows. Trees shade winding paths. Gravestones stand in orderly lines. But in late spring and early summer, the ground in certain sections comes alive in a different way. Tiny holes dot the soil, each one the entrance to a bee nest. From these openings, thousands of small, dark bees emerge and return in a constant, low hum.The bees are ground-nesting species, meaning they dig their nests into bare or sparsely vegetated soil rather than building hives in trees or man-made structures. Many people associate bees with honey-producing colonies in wooden boxes, but the majority of wild bee species are solitary or live in small family groups, and a large share of them nest in the ground. The cemetery, with its open, well-drained lawns and limited pesticide use, turns out to be an ideal place for them to raise their young.How researchers counted the uncountableCounting millions of tiny, fast-moving insects is not a simple task. The research team, led by scientists from Cornell University, used a combination of field surveys, statistical modelling and extrapolation to arrive at their estimate. They began by mapping the areas of the cemetery in which bee nests were concentrated, and within those areas, they estimated nest density by counting the number of nest entrances in sample plots of known size. They then factored in data on how many female bees typically occupy a single nest and how many offspring each female produces over a nesting season. By combining nest density, nest occupancy and reproductive rates, they were able to estimate the total number of individual bees using the 1.5-acre study area over the course of a season. The result, about 5.5 million bees, is an estimate rather than an exact count, but it is grounded in rigorous sampling and peer-reviewed methods.Why so many bees in such a small spaceSeveral features of the cemetery make it unusually favourable for ground-nesting bees. The soil is well drained and relatively compact, which helps nests stay stable and dry. Regular mowing keeps the vegetation short and creates patches of bare ground that many of the bee species prefer for nesting. At the same time, the surrounding landscape provides a steady supply of flowers, from early spring blooms to late summer wildflowers, so that adult bees have enough nectar and pollen to feed themselves and their larvae. Importantly, the cemetery is managed with minimal pesticide use. Many urban and suburban lawns are treated with insecticides and herbicides that can kill bees directly or reduce the availability of flowering plants. In this cemetery, the management approach prioritises long term landscape stability and low chemical inputs, creating a safer environment for nesting insects.The result is a place where bees can reproduce in extraordinary numbers without conflicting heavily with human activities. Visitors may notice the bees, especially on warm, sunny days, but the insects are generally non-aggressive and focused on foraging and nest building rather than defending a large communal hive.The finding in the Ithaca cemetery has gotten attention because it flies in the face of common stories about where wildlife can find refuge in human-made landscapes. Cities and towns are often thought to be inhospitable to native bees, which are thought to require large swaths of natural habitat to thrive.This study shows that even small, seemingly mundane patches of green space can support massive populations if they are managed in a bee-friendly way. Cemeteries, parks, school grounds and other open spaces are scattered throughout urban areas. If managed with nesting habitat and floral resources in mind, they could function as a network of refuges for wild bees. The sheer number of bees found in just 1.5 acres implies that the total bee biomass in such landscapes could be far larger than previously recognised.For conservationists, the takeaway is not that all cemeteries should be left unmanaged, but that modest changes in mowing schedules, pesticide policies and soil disturbance can make a big difference. Leaving some areas of bare ground, reducing chemical inputs and planting native flowering species can turn ordinary lawns into productive bee habitat.Importance of ground-nesting bees to ecosystemsGround-nesting bees are important pollinators. Many are generalist foragers, visiting a wide range of wildflowers, garden plants and crops. Some are specialists, only visiting a few plant species within a family, forging close ecological links that support plant diversity. They tend to forage near their nests and thus provide very localised pollination services to plants near their colonies.Most ground-nesting bees are solitary or live in small groups, unlike honey bees that are social and live in large perennial colonies. Females construct and provision their own nests, laying eggs in individual cells provisioned with pollen and nectar. This life history renders them especially susceptible to disruptions at the nest site, such as frequent tilling, high foot traffic or pesticide use that contaminates the soil.The presence of millions of these bees in a single site underscores how critical undisturbed ground is to their survival, as well as the potential for human-managed landscapes to support not just a few isolated nests but entire population strongholds.Implications for bee conservation and land managementThe Ithaca study comes at a time when wild bee populations are threatened by habitat loss, pesticide exposure, disease and climate change. Many conservation efforts focus on planting pollinator gardens or installing bee hotels, which may help some species but do not meet the needs of ground nesters. This research suggests that protecting and creating suitable nesting substrate is equally important. Land managers in urban and suburban areas can take several lessons from the cemetery example. Reducing the frequency and intensity of soil disturbance, limiting pesticide use and maintaining a mosaic of mowed and unmowed areas can all support ground-nesting bees. Even small adjustments, such as leaving some patches of bare soil along edges or under trees, can provide nesting opportunities.At the policy level, the findings encourage a broader view of green infrastructure. Cemeteries, utility corridors, roadside verges and other overlooked spaces could be incorporated into pollinator conservation plans, not just as sources of flowers but as nesting habitat. Recognising that millions of bees can live beneath our feet in places we walk every day may help shift public perception of what counts as valuable nature.A quiet miracle beneath the gravestonesFor the researchers walking among the headstones, the project was as humbling as it was fascinating. A vibrant, hidden world had been thriving underfoot the entire time, completely unnoticed.Finding 5.5 million bees living beneath just 1.5 acres of cemetery grass isn't a problem to solve; it is proof that nature can flourish inside manicured human spaces. It also points to a huge, untapped opportunity for towns everywhere. If a quiet cemetery in upstate New York can support a population that size, rethinking how we manage our everyday parks, yards, and lawns could easily give these underground communities room to thrive.

articles.title: Southern California anglers are catching unusually large fish rarely seen this far north as Pacific waters warm
articles.summary: Wildlife & Biodiversity News: Southern California anglers are seeing an unusual number of warm-water fish as rising ocean temperatures linked to El Niño and marine heatwaves bring .
articles.body: Southern California anglers are seeing an unusual number of warm-water fish as rising ocean temperatures linked to El Niño and marine heatwaves bring species typically found farther south into local waters.Fishermen working in Marina del Rey and Santa Monica are catching fish species, in larger sizes, that are rarely seen in the area. Tony Villanueva, a boat captain who has been operating out of the area for years, describes the haul as unprecedented.“Biggest yellowtail I've ever seen up here,” Villanueva told ABC 7.Another captain, Alex Garcia, also said that anglers have been getting unusually large catches. “We've been catching a bunch of big bonito,” Garcia said.These species of fish are often seen in waters off Mexico, but now they are appearing along the Southern California coast.“People go on overnight trips and pay big money to go catch the fish that we're catching right here, right in our backyard,” Garcia added.Ocean temperatures off Southern California have risen well above normal due to a marine heatwave overlapping with El Niño conditions. Dr Julia Coates, an environmental scientist with the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, told the broadcaster that warmer ocean conditions are driving these changes.“Right now we're experiencing warm water due to what's called a marine heatwave,” the scientist told the outlet.She explained that the marine heatwave is bringing unusually warm water to Southern California, drawing tropical and pelagic species that typically inhabit deeper waters. These unusual conditions have resulted in these rare sightings for local anglers. “To see a hammerhead shark with yellowtails swimming around it was pretty cool.”Boat captains who have spent decades fishing in the local waters have called it a rare event.“We had fish up to, like, 25, almost pushing 30 pounds. Unheard of here, unheard of. Dorado, catching dorado on the anchor right off Santa Monica,” Villanueva said.Garcia observed that water temperatures are significantly higher than normal. “The water temperature obviously is way higher than it usually is. It's like 76 degrees out there.”The temporary abundance is exciting; however, it may upend local fishing economics. Coates added that warmer waters have boosted fishing opportunities; similar conditions in the past have had serious environmental consequences. “We saw a dramatic loss of kelp and kelp forests in Northern CA, that ecosystem was dramatically changed and has not yet recovered,” Coates explained, referring to the previous thermal anomaly.Villanueva also commented on the effects of unusually warm water farther south. “Down south, the water's so warm that it's actually killing off some fish because the water's too warm.”Coates also cautioned against viewing the fish boom as simple good fortune. Between 2013 and 2016, Southern California experienced a similar collision of El Niño and extended marine heatwaves during an event called ‘The Blob’. Local fishing operators have plans to continue running trips despite expectations for high surf. “The fish are out there, it's a really cool time to get out on the water,” Garcia said.

articles.title: Scientists discovered an underwater city of 20,000 octopus nests deep inside California coast; largest known nursery on the planet
articles.summary: Wildlife & Biodiversity News: Researchers have located the planet's largest known octopus nursery deep off the Californian coast, documenting 5,718 animals in 2.5 hectares and esti.
articles.body: Researchers have located the planet's largest known octopus nursery deep off the Californian coast, documenting 5,718 animals in 2.5 hectares and estimating about 20,000 around Davidson Seamount. Known as the Octopus Garden, the nursery is located about 10,500 feet below the surface off Central California. According to a statement released by the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute (MBARI) on August 23, 2023, monitoring confirmed that pearl octopuses migrate to the site for mating and nesting.The Octopus GardenThe nursery is situated on a small hill near the base of the Davidson Seamount, which is an extinct volcano located 130 kilometres southwest of Monterey, California. The large concentration first drew attention in October 2018. Researchers from the Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary, NOAA, Ocean Exploration Trust, and collaborators, working aboard the E/V Nautilus, observed thousands of octopuses gathered on a rocky rise near the seamount.The position of the animals helped researchers understand exactly what was happening in the section of the ocean. Many of the octopuses were upside down, with their arms positioned around their bodies, a posture that is associated with females protecting and incubating their eggs.The species was identified as Muusoctopus robustus, known to researchers as the pearl octopus. They exhibit a pale purple colouration. According to MBARI, the animal is approximately the size of a grapefruit and occurs in the northeastern Pacific Ocean, from Oregon down to Baja California. The institute has observed the species at depths between 2,300 and 3,600 metres.Research on the nurseryAfter the initial discovery, researchers began a prolonged investigation to determine why so many animals were concentrated at that point. For three years, the institute and its partner institutions employed cameras, sensors, remotely operated vehicles and other equipment to observe the behaviour of octopuses and the environmental conditions of the nursery.Doc Ricketts, a remotely operated vehicle from MBARI, played a central role in the research. The team conducted 14 dives with the ROV during which scientists found adult males and females, developing eggs and hatchlings. No individuals of intermediate size or evidence of feeding were observed at the site. These observations indicated that the octopuses gather there specifically to mate and nest. The size of the concentration was measured using a combination of photographs and detailed mapping of the seabed. The LASS system, installed on the Doc Ricketts ROV, allowed high-resolution images to be produced and a photomosaic of the region to be assembled. In this survey, researchers documented 5,718 octopuses in just 2.5 hectares at the centre of the Octopus Garden. The slight elevation where the nursery is located occupies approximately 333 hectares, or 823 acres. Based on the surveys conducted, the team calculated that the total population could easily exceed 20,000 individuals.It is the thermal conditions of the area that explain why this small area attracts so many animals. At approximately 3,200 meters, the normal water temperature is around 1.6°C. However, in the crevices and fissures used by the octopuses, water warmed by the hydrothermal vents reaches nearly 11°C. The initial researchers observed a "sparkling" appearance in the water, caused by the mixture of hot and cold water. Subsequent investigations confirmed the existence of hydrothermal vents and showed that the nests are clustered precisely in the fissures bathed by the warmer water emerging from the seabed.Why this region?Octopuses are ectothermic animals, and the cold deep waters reduce their metabolism and slow embryonic development. At temperatures close to zero found in the abyssal environment, researchers expected that the pearl octopus's eggs would need five to eight years or even longer to hatch.But the temperature in these locations revealed a different outcome. Using 4K imaging and features like scars to recognise the animals, scientists tracked their clutches and found that the eggs hatched in less than two years. This acceleration was attributed to the heat from he hydrothermal vents, which increases the mothers' and embryos' metabolism. The longer the incubation, the greater the period during which the embryos are subject to predation, injury, infections, and other sources of mortality.Females migrate to the Octopus Garden in search of warm locations where they can nest. Each one lays a clutch of approximately 60 elongated eggs and covers the embryos with her body while they develop.Interestingly, the nursery also serves as a food source for other species. As is typically the case with cephalopods, both male and female pearl octopuses die after reproduction. Most mother remain alive until the eggs hatch, though some exhaust their reserves before development is complete. Their carcasses are consumed by various organisms from the area. Ratfish, cusk eels, sea slugs, anemones, and other scavengers take advantage of the remains left after reproduction. Researchers estimated that this biomass provides 72% more food to the local marine community than would be available outside the Octopus Garden.The Octopus Garden is described by MBARI as the largest known concentration of octopuses on the planet to date.

articles.title: Scientists removed more than 70% of underwater logs from one half of a Wisconsin lake; within 2 years its once-dominant yellow perch population had nearly disappeared
articles.summary: Nature & Environment News: From the surface a lake might look like it is not changing at all but underneath it is a very different story. Scientists demonstrated how important f.
articles.body: From the surface a lake might look like it is not changing at all but underneath it is a very different story. Scientists demonstrated how important fallen trees and submerged logs can be to freshwater ecosystems in an unusual whole-lake experiment under calm waters of Wisconsin’s Little Rock Lake. In the study, ‘The rapid effects of a whole-lake reduction of coarse woody debris on fish and benthic macroinvertebrates’, researchers removed over 70% of the coarse woody habitat from one basin of the lake, and the effects were quickly seen in its fish. Yellow perch, which was once the lake’s most abundant fish, plummeted to very low numbers within two years, the study adds. The study was conducted in Little Rock Lake, an 18-hectare undeveloped, unfished lake in Vilas County, Wisconsin. A large curtain divides the lake into 2 similar basins. Fish and water cannot pass between the basins. That unusual setup gave researchers a natural laboratory setting. One basin was designated as the treatment area in which approximately 70% of the coarse woody debris along the shallow shore was removed in 2002. The other basin was left as a control. The aim was to determine what happens when a key feature of the habitat is removed.Why underwater logs are importantFallen trees and branches might appear to be nothing more than debris but they create complex underwater environments. Logs provide fish with places to hide, feed and shelter and also increase the variety of habitat available in the lake. The two basins had broadly similar food webs dominated by aquatic prey before the experiment. But after removal of the woody habitat, the fish community started to respond differently.Decline of yellow perchThe most striking change was the decline in yellow perch, which had been the most abundant fish species in the lake. Perch densities in the treatment basin dropped to very low levels. Researchers attributed the decline to increased predation and little or no successful recruitment of young fish. It was a stark contrast to the pristine basin. In the reference basin, yellow perch produced several generations of young in successive years, thus rebuilding the population. Thus, woody cover loss appeared to influence where fish were found and their ability to survive and maintain populations.Bass altered their behaviorLargemouth bass also responded to the changed habitat. After log removal, bass in the treatment basin consumed less fish and relied more on terrestrial prey. Their growth also slowed relative to bass in the reference basin. The results suggest that removing underwater structure can alter predator-prey relationships across an entire ecosystem, not just impact a single species in isolation.Not every species responded immediatelyOddly the experiment did not produce the same rapid changes in aquatic invertebrates. There was no significant difference in the composition, diversity or density of benthic macroinvertebrate communities between the treatment and reference basins during the two years following the habitat reduction. That contrast illustrates how different parts of an ecosystem can respond at very different speeds.A warning for developed coastsThe findings have implications beyond Little Rock Lake. As shorelines are developed, riparian forests may be thinned and fallen trees removed from shallow water for esthetic or recreational reasons. The experiment shows that such small changes can have big implications for fish communities. The study, Fish Community and Food Web Responses to a Whole-Lake Removal of Coarse Woody Habitat, shows that keeping submerged woody habitat is important to support desirable fish populations and healthy fisheries. What looks like clutter from above may be, below the surface, critical infrastructure for an entire aquatic food web.Images Courtesy: Wikipedia

articles.title: In 2021, a North Yorkshire estate began restoring 2,500 acres of intensively farmed land; four years later, 330,000 trees and 1,700+ species mark its comeback
articles.summary: Nature & Environment News: Four years after moving 2,500 acres of North Yorkshire farmland away from intensive farming, conservation teams at Broughton Sanctuary have recorded m.
articles.body: Four years after moving 2,500 acres of North Yorkshire farmland away from intensive farming, conservation teams at Broughton Sanctuary have recorded more than 1,700 species and planted 330,000 trees across the estate. According to the Broughton Sanctuary State of Nature Recovery Report, published in December 2025, 80 per cent of the 1,030-hectare historic site near Skipton is now managed through rewilding and nature-friendly farming methods. The land was previously mainly used as monoculture pasture. Supported by the White Rose Forest through the UK Government's Trees for Climate programme, tree cover across the estate rose from less than 5 per cent in 2020 to more than 35 per cent by the end of 2025.Woodland expansion and species countsThe estate's tree-planting programme has added 19 native broadleaf species across 400 hectares. These young woodland corridors link areas of broken-up habitat, helping wildlife move between them while also supporting carbon capture and natural flood management. Surveys included in the report have recorded more than 1,700 species across the restored land. Reduced intensive grazing allowed longer grasses to grow, leading to an increase in small mammals and attracting more birds of prey. All five native British owl species now live at the sanctuary: Barn, Tawny, Little, Long-eared and Short-eared owls. Field observations suggest Short-eared Owls are almost certainly breeding on the estate for the first time in decades. Other birds of prey recorded include Peregrine Falcons, Merlins, Hen Harriers, Red Kites and Sparrowhawks. To help birds of prey nest, conservationists installed 13 Barn Owl boxes and 13 Kestrel boxes supplied by specialist Colin Shawyer. Monitoring carried out with Stephen Downing of the Northern England Raptor Forum recorded 33 Barn Owl chicks and 13 Kestrel chicks ringed in 2024. A long spring drought in 2025 reduced vole numbers and delayed nesting, but late-summer broods recovered, leading to six more Barn Owl chicks being ringed. Alongside broadleaf planting, the estate worked with Benedict Pollard of Mighty Fine Oaks to plant 76 specimen oaks in the registered parkland. The trees were grown from acorns collected from historic British trees. The project aims to protect genetic diversity and create a supply of veteran trees for future generations.Habitat engineering through livestockNatural changes across the estate are also being driven by carefully managed livestock grazing. The sanctuary currently has 57 Riggit Galloway cattle, three Iron Age pigs, three Dales ponies and 15 Roe Deer. The Riggit Galloway cattle are managed with local farmer Neil Heseltine of Hill Top Farm in Malham and remain outdoors throughout the year. They graze without chemical treatments, regular medication or silage, helping stop aggressive plant species from taking over open grassland. The three Iron Age pigs were introduced in August 2024 and act as natural soil engineers. Their rooting breaks up compacted ground, exposing old seedbeds and creating patches of bare soil. Botanical monitoring found new plants growing in these disturbed areas, including Common Eyebright, Sneezewort, Creeping Cinquefoil, Bird's-foot Trefoil and Mouse-ear Hawkweed. Self-seeded birch, oak and cherry saplings were also recorded. Thistles growing in the disturbed areas provided nectar for pollinators late in the season and attracted groups of Goldfinches feeding on their seed heads. In wet areas, a family of beavers made up of two adults and one kit continues to change local watercourses. Their dams hold water across the landscape, create wetland areas and slow the flow of streams during storms.Infrastructure changes and future targetsPhysical barriers across the sanctuary have also been changed to help animals move more freely. Teams removed 17 kilometres of fencing, creating connected routes through pasture, woodland and moorland. Water management work included creating seven wetland scrapes and ponds to hold water on floodplains. A 30-kilometre trail network, called the Odyssey Nature Trail, was opened to give the public access to selected nature recovery areas. Figures in the report show that 200 local volunteers helped with habitat management during 2025. Educational programmes brought 7,331 children to the site for school visits, while general public activities reached 1,500 people during the year. The number of staff working on nature recovery also increased from two full-time positions to seven. The report's 10-year plan sets out further goals for the period from 2026 to 2036. Planned work includes expanding wetlands created by beavers, developing self-sustaining herds of rare-breed livestock and restoring floodplains by reversing old drainage ditches. Estate managers also plan to bring back native species that are missing from the area, starting with the Harvest Mouse in 2026. Other work will focus on restoring moorland, planting gullies and gradually removing non-native plants such as Rhododendron and Laurel from existing forests.

articles.title: EcoFlow makes the miniature power station even smaller
articles.summary: EcoFlow’s River 520 Gen4 and 260 Gen feature class leading energy density allowing these power stations to punch well above their size.
articles.body: If you’re in the market for a tiny power station that punches well above its size and weight then have a look at EcoFlow’s new fourth-generation River series. The River 260 Gen4 features a 256Wh capacity battery while the 520 Gen4 packs in 512Wh — storing about 2.5x and 5x the energy of the largest airline-approved power banks, respectively. Better yet, the batteries are built using longer-lasting LFP chemistry that’s far less volatile. The River 260 Gen4 features four USB ports, and 300W of max continuous output delivered out its lone AC jack. The River 500 Gen4 features the same USB port selection but offers a pair of AC jacks good for 500W of continuous output. Both of EcoFlow’s Gen4 power stations feature class-leading energy density that cuts both the weight and size, making these power stations lighter and more compact than similarly-specced competition. That makes them ideal for an overnight camping trip or photo shoot in the literal field. The EcoFlow 520 Gen4 is powerful enough to keep a standard US fridge running for about 4 hours during a blackout. [Image: [Image: Here’s a quick comparison to show just how much energy these remarkably small power stations are packing, starting with the River 520 Gen4: And here’s how the River 260 Gen4 compares to some of the main competition: Both models can serve as a UPS for your computer, with a cutover time of less than 10ms, and feature one state-of-the-art 140W USB-C PD3.1 port that’s bidirectional. That little trick lets these power stations eschew charging bricks in favor of direct DC charging from a 140W USB-C wall charger you might already own, or a portable USB-C solar panel EcoFlow will happily sell you. EcoFlow has also addressed a common problem with all power stations that causes them to eventually die if left idling too long. By minimizing the energy spent converting stored DC to AC output, more watt-hours remain to charge your drone, bike computer, and phone, or to power your Starlink Mini and compact fridge. The River 260 Gen4 will be available in Europe from Q4 2026, while the River 520 Gen4 will follow sometimes in Q1 2027. Pricing for both will be announced as we get closer to their global release dates.

articles.title: In 2023, Australia put a 330-square-metre floating wetland on a wastewater lagoon; two years later researchers found methane emissions had fallen by up to 66%
articles.summary: Nature & Environment News: Installing a floating wetland planted with native vegetation on an Australian municipal wastewater lagoon cut methane emissions by up to 66 per cent, .
articles.body: Installing a floating wetland planted with native vegetation on an Australian municipal wastewater lagoon cut methane emissions by up to 66 per cent, according to the results of a two-year field trial. Published on 25 August 2026 in the Journal of Environmental Management, the peer-reviewed study looked at how constructed floating wetlands affect greenhouse gas emissions from open water storage. The trial was carried out at a Westernport Water treatment facility on Phillip Island, Victoria, by researchers from RMIT University, Australia's national science agency CSIRO, and Westernport Water. The trial measured emissions continuously using "Pondi", a solar-powered sensor system developed by RMIT with partners from Deakin University, The University of Queensland and Leading Edge Engineering Solutions. During the monitoring period, carbon dioxide emissions fell by up to 36 per cent, while nitrous oxide levels dropped by 18 per cent compared with a control lagoon without a floating platform. Wastewater treatment around the world produces about 1.6 per cent of human-caused greenhouse gas emissions. Much of this comes from high nutrient levels that encourage gas-producing microbes to grow in stagnant ponds.Native plants and sub-surface root dynamicsFor the trial, researchers installed a 330-square-metre floating platform, about the size of one and a half tennis courts. It was planted with Australian native wetland species, including Phragmites australis, Baumea articulata and Bolboschoenus caldwellii. As the reeds and sedges grew on the floating pontoons, their roots extended directly into the nutrient-rich water below. The site needed regular maintenance to remove invasive weeds and manage local bird populations, but the roots quickly developed complex habitats for microbes and other organisms. Dr Lukas Schuster, lead author of the study and a researcher at RMIT University, said the root systems supported useful microbial communities that could process pollutants and gases in the water. “This is the first time we've had evidence on this scale that supporting microbial communities in the root systems of wetland plants can reduce wastewater emissions without relying on high-tech solutions,” Dr Lukas Schuster said. “It's a strong demonstration of how nature-based approaches can transform wastewater treatment into part of the climate solution.” Clear reductions in greenhouse gas emissions were seen four months after the platform was installed, even though overall nutrient levels in the water remained largely unchanged during the study.Decarbonising water sector infrastructureThe methane cuts recorded during the Phillip Island trial could be useful for water utilities working towards net-zero targets. Although methane remains in the atmosphere for less time than carbon dioxide, it has a much stronger warming effect over shorter periods. Open wastewater lagoons often have low-oxygen conditions that speed up the breakdown of organic matter and methane production. This means simple ways to reduce emissions can be difficult to introduce across municipal water systems. Dona Tantirimudalige, Managing Director at Westernport Water, said floating platforms could allow utilities to improve existing treatment facilities without major rebuilding work. “The outcomes provide a strong foundation for further work to test performance across additional lagoon types and operating conditions,” Dona Tantirimudalige said. “Building this evidence base is important for utilities as we continue to develop credible and cost-effective emissions abatement pathways.” Researchers also found that the plant roots could work as natural filters, taking in heavy metals and suspended pollutants before treated water flows into nearby marine or freshwater areas.Scaling biological platforms across agricultural sitesAfter the results from the municipal wastewater lagoon, water researchers at RMIT's Centre for Nature Positive Solutions began wider trials across regional Victoria. Working with Melbourne Water and the Bass Coast Landcare Network, researchers are placing floating wetland pods in farm dams across the Bass Coast. Australia has an estimated 1.8 million farm dams, which together are a significant source of agricultural methane because of livestock runoff and stagnant water. Dr Martino Malerba, a co-author of the study and RMIT water researcher, said biological water treatment methods could be used in many different settings. “Floating wetlands harness the power of nature to help restore balance in aquatic systems,” Dr Martino Malerba said. “By supporting microbial communities in the root systems of wetland plants, we can improve water quality without relying on high-tech solutions.” Testing on regional farm dams is still underway to find out whether similar reductions in emissions and improvements in water quality can be achieved across privately owned agricultural properties.

articles.title: China tested nanobubbles across a 3,300-square-metre section of Taihu Lake; within 20 days a key measure of cyanobacteria fell nearly 90% and ammonia nitrogen dropped sharply
articles.summary: Nature & Environment News: A field trial using a two-stage nanobubble treatment system across a 3,300-square-metre section of Taihu Lake in eastern China reduced a key measure o.
articles.body: A field trial using a two-stage nanobubble treatment system across a 3,300-square-metre section of Taihu Lake in eastern China reduced a key measure of toxic cyanobacteria by nearly 90 per cent within 20 days. Published in the journal Environmental Research and indexed on PubMed, the peer-reviewed study describes an in-situ restoration project aimed at controlling harmful algal blooms and improving water clarity in one of China's largest freshwater lakes. The treatment combined hydrodynamic cavitation with ozone nanobubbles in a semi-enclosed test area. Water quality monitoring showed that chlorophyll-a, a key indicator of cyanobacteria levels, fell by 89.8 per cent during the three-week trial. Severe cyanobacterial blooms have affected Taihu Lake for decades. Agricultural runoff, industrial discharge and urban wastewater across the Yangtze River Delta have helped drive the problem. These blooms reduce dissolved oxygen, release toxic microcystins and threaten drinking water supplies for millions of people in Jiangsu and Zhejiang provinces.Dual-stage physical and chemical treatmentTraditional methods of treating polluted water, such as using copper sulfate or mechanically removing algae, can be difficult to use across large areas. They can also create additional chemical pollution. To address these problems, researchers used a mobile treatment platform that produces tiny gas bubbles directly in the water. Nanobubbles are less than 200 nanometres wide. Unlike larger bubbles, which quickly rise to the surface and burst, they can remain suspended in water for weeks. This allows gases to move into the water more efficiently and supports a range of physical and chemical reactions. The first stage used hydrodynamic cavitation, which creates strong forces in the water that damage cyanobacterial cells and break their gas vesicles. This causes the algae to lose buoyancy and sink. The second stage added ozone-filled nanobubbles. When these bubbles collapsed, they produced hydroxyl radicals that broke down organic pollutants and remaining algal toxins without adding synthetic chemicals.Rapid chemical and biological recoveryWater samples collected during the 20-day trial showed major reductions in chemical pollutants and nutrients across the 3,300-square-metre treatment area. Ammonia nitrogen levels fell sharply, reducing one of the main factors that contributes to eutrophication and repeated seasonal blooms. Total phosphorus and chemical oxygen demand also decreased, while dissolved oxygen levels steadily increased as the nanobubbles carried oxygen deeper into the water. Higher oxygen levels helped stabilise bottom sediments and reduced the chance of stored nutrients being released back into the lake. Water transparency also improved significantly. Clearer water allowed more sunlight to reach the lakebed, supporting the natural recovery of submerged aquatic plants.Scaling up ecological restorationTaihu Lake lies between Jiangsu and Zhejiang provinces and covers more than 2,200 square kilometres. Its shallow basin makes it especially vulnerable to summer algal blooms linked to high temperatures. The problem gained international attention in 2007, when a major blue-green algae outbreak forced Wuxi to shut down parts of its municipal water supply. Since the 2007 crisis, regional authorities have spent billions of yuan on environmental restoration. Measures have included removing polluted sediment, expanding sewage networks and introducing stricter limits on industrial discharges. Nanobubble technology represents a move towards more targeted, high-tech methods of managing polluted water. The research team said the low energy use and efficient transfer of gases make two-stage nanobubble systems suitable for larger bays and tributaries. Further long-term monitoring is planned to determine how well water quality improvements continue after active nanobubble treatment is stopped.

articles.title: Scientists covered 200 square metres of a Swiss glacier with sheep’s wool; early tests found it protected the ice about as well as plastic sheets, but only 0.02% of Swiss glacier ice is covered
articles.summary: Earth & Climate News: A natural wool covering placed over 200 square metres of high-altitude Alpine ice has proved as effective at slowing summer melting as conventional sy.
articles.body: A natural wool covering placed over 200 square metres of high-altitude Alpine ice has proved as effective at slowing summer melting as conventional synthetic tarpaulins, offering a possible biodegradable alternative to plastic sheets. Initial results from the "Keep It Wool" trial on the Tsanfleuron Glacier in western Switzerland show that prototype wool blankets protected snow and ice from heat about as well as plastic geotextiles. According to a Reuters report published on 3 September 2026, researchers found that the covers significantly slowed ice loss during the warmer summer months. However, project organisers and glaciologists stress that physical covers can only protect very small areas. Just about 0.02 per cent of Switzerland's total glacier surface is currently covered with protective materials. This means the method is mainly useful for protecting ski areas or vulnerable infrastructure, rather than providing a wider solution to global warming.Coverings shield only a minute fraction of Swiss ice: Total Swiss Glacier Area: 99.98% Uncovered Area Under Protective Covers: 0.02%Shepherds and scientists unite on high iceThe experiment at the Glacier 3000 resort near Les Diablerets was first proposed by four master's students. It was later developed into a joint project involving the environmental organisation Summit Foundation, the University of Lausanne and the Swiss Glacier Monitoring Network (Glamos). In June, researchers placed two 100-square-metre wool blankets next to standard synthetic covers. This allowed them to compare the two materials directly in real Alpine conditions. The wool panels were made by Swiss textile company Fisolan. Measurements taken every two weeks throughout the summer showed that the wool blankets reduced ice loss by about the same amount as synthetic covers. These conventional covers usually cut local melting by 50 to 70 per cent. "I thought it wouldn't be stable enough," said Niklaus Zegeser of Fisolan, who said he was surprised by how well the natural fibre survived strong winds, heavy rain and freezing temperature changes. Eliot Gaffio, one of the student researchers, said the field team was relieved when the summer results arrived. "Now we have a result that we can see and even touch. It worked incredibly well," Gaffio said.Replacing plastic with discarded agricultural wasteFor years, Alpine resorts in Switzerland, Austria and Italy have used large geotextile tarpaulins to cover important sections of glaciers during summer. The covers reflect sunlight and reduce heat transfer, but almost all conventional sheets are made from synthetic plastics such as polyethylene or PVC. Long exposure to strong ultraviolet light and wind can damage these plastic covers. As they break down, they can release tiny synthetic fibres into meltwater, streams and nearby soils. The search for a natural alternative led researchers to an agricultural byproduct that is widely available. Project manager Timothy Steiner said the team wanted to create a fully biodegradable cover while finding a useful purpose for Swiss sheep's wool. Between 40 and 70 per cent of the wool is regularly thrown away or burned each year because there is little commercial demand for it. By turning an unused local material into a protective sheet for high-altitude ice, the project shows how agricultural waste could be reused in local climate adaptation efforts.Extreme melt season highlights systemic limitsThe trial took place as ice loss continues to accelerate across the European Alps. Unusually high summer temperatures caused winter snow reserves to disappear weeks earlier than normal, exposing darker glacier ice to sunlight much earlier in the season. Glacier retreat can also make high mountain slopes less stable, increasing the risk of landslides and rockfalls. This includes the major rockfall that damaged the Swiss village of Blatten in 2025. Melting glaciers can also affect water supplies further downstream during different seasons. Despite the success of the wool prototype, scientists warn that glacier blankets should not be seen as a solution to climate change. Glaciologists point out that protective covers are expensive to install, require significant labour to maintain and can only be used on small areas of high-value ice. Steiner and the scientific teams involved stressed that physical covers cannot replace rapid cuts in global greenhouse gas emissions. Sheep's wool could help keep microplastics out of Alpine meltwater, but reducing fossil fuel use remains the only long-term way to slow the loss of the world's glaciers and ice sheets.Swiss scientists test wool to protect glaciersA Reuters video report provides visual context on the 200-square-metre wool blankets installed on the Tsanfleuron Glacier alongside standard synthetic covers, with comments from members of the research team.

articles.title: In 1952, Mary Tsingou programmed a Los Alamos experiment that helped change modern physics; her role was reduced to a footnote and took more than 50 years to receive proper credit
articles.summary: Experiments & Discoveries News: When mathematician and programmer Mary Tsingou Menzel sat down in 1952 at Los Alamos National Laboratory to code a complex physics problem on one of t.
articles.body: When mathematician and programmer Mary Tsingou Menzel sat down in 1952 at Los Alamos National Laboratory to code a complex physics problem on one of the world’s earliest digital computers, she was breaking new ground. Her work helped make possible a landmark experiment that went on to influence chaos theory, non-linear dynamics and modern scientific computing. Yet when the findings were published in a major 1955 paper, her name was missing from the title page and appeared only in a sentence at the bottom of the front page: "We wish to thank Miss Mary Tsingou for running the computations on the Los Alamos MANIAC machine." It took more than half a century for the scientific community to formally recognise her contribution. Following her death on 27 August 2026 at her home in Los Alamos, New Mexico, aged 97, obituaries in major publications including The Washington Post and the Los Alamos Daily Post highlighted her important role in 20th-century physics. Born to Greek immigrant parents in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, on 14 October 1928, Tsingou earned a bachelor’s degree in mathematics from the University of Wisconsin in 1951 before joining Los Alamos. At the time, female mathematicians were paid less than male colleagues because employers openly argued that men were the main breadwinners.Turning equations into computer codeTsingou was assigned to the laboratory’s Theoretical Division, where dozens of women worked as manual "computers", carrying out routine calculations on mechanical desktop calculators. But her technical skills soon led to her becoming one of the first programmers of the MANIAC (Mathematical Analyzer, Numerical Integrator, and Computer), a huge room-sized machine built under the direction of Nicholas Metropolis. Working with leading theoretical physicists Enrico Fermi, John Pasta and Stanisław Ulam, Tsingou was asked to code a non-linear string oscillation problem to study how energy moved through the system over time. The physicists developed the equations but did not have the programming skills needed to run them on the new machine. "They didn't know anything about programming," Tsingou said in an oral history interview recorded for the IEEE Global History Network. "They set up the equations, and I did all the programming." Tsingou wrote the code line by line on punch cards, carefully checking her work before putting them into the MANIAC. The computer ran for hours and produced a result that surprised the researchers. Instead of spreading energy evenly as expected under statistical mechanics, the system returned to its original energy state in a repeating pattern. The unexpected result changed theoretical physics and led to decades of research into non-linear systems and soliton theory.From footnote to full recognitionWhen the study was released as a Los Alamos report in May 1955, shortly after Fermi’s death, it listed Fermi, Pasta and Ulam as the main authors. Tsingou was mentioned only in a footnote for carrying out the computations. For decades, the experiment became widely known as the Fermi-Pasta-Ulam (FPU) problem. University textbooks, academic papers and scientific conferences continued to use the three men’s names, while Tsingou’s role remained largely unknown. That began to change in 2008, when French physicist Thierry Dauxois published a paper in Physics Today titled "Fermi, Pasta, Ulam, and a mysterious lady." Dauxois argued that, under modern academic standards, Tsingou’s contribution was important enough to deserve full authorship. "It is time for a proper recognition of her decisive contribution," Dauxois wrote, suggesting that the problem should be renamed the Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou (FPUT) problem. The scientific community gradually adopted the new name, formally adding Tsingou to the title more than 50 years after she first ran the code.A quiet pioneer of computingTsingou completed a master’s degree in applied mathematics from the University of Michigan in 1955 before returning to Los Alamos. She worked there for 35 years before retiring. She later married Joseph Menzel and became an early expert in Fortran, developing algorithms used to simulate nuclear weapons effects, explosions and fluid dynamics. She is also credited with co-creating one of the earliest computer graphics programmes capable of showing physical explosions visually on a screen. Despite the later campaign to give her proper academic credit, colleagues remembered Tsingou Menzel as a modest person who rarely focused on her historic role. She often spoke with pride about serving her country during the Cold War through national security science. She is survived by her two daughters, Ann and Carol, both medical doctors. Her work on the MANIAC machine remains an important milestone in the history of computational physics.

articles.title: Scientists tagged 14,000 endangered Australian moths with paint and eyelash glue to trace their migration; not one was found, and researchers say that may be good news
articles.summary: Science News: More than 14,000 Bogong moths were tagged in an unusual attempt to uncover the secrets of one of Australia’s most remarkable insect migrations. Resear.
articles.body: More than 14,000 Bogong moths were tagged in an unusual attempt to uncover the secrets of one of Australia’s most remarkable insect migrations. Researchers marked the endangered moths in the Snowy Mountains and hoped to track where they travelled after leaving their summer shelters. Some were marked with non-toxic paint, while others were fitted with tiny paper tags attached to their wings. According to ABC News, volunteers released the tagged moths around Mount Kosciuszko and used light traps to look for them as they moved through the region. Yet, despite the large number of insects tagged, not a single one has been found so far. Researchers say that may not necessarily mean the project failed. The absence of tagged moths could indicate that the population is larger than expected or that the insects are following a different migration route.A mysterious annual migrationBogong moths are known for undertaking one of Australia's most remarkable insect migrations. Every year, billions of these peanut-sized moths travel to the cooler regions of the New South Wales Snowy Mountains, including the caves around Mount Kosciuszko, to escape the heat. When conditions change, the moths leave their mountain shelters and travel thousands of kilometres back towards inland areas where they breed. However, scientists still do not have a complete picture of exactly where the moths go or which routes they use.That uncertainty is particularly important because Bogong moths have experienced a dramatic decline. Their population fell by as much as 99.5 per cent during a major crash in 2017 associated with drought and climate change. The species was listed as endangered in 2021. Researchers from Western Sydney University and Invertebrates Australia launched the tagging project to gain a clearer understanding of the moths' movements and help improve conservation efforts.Tiny tags and eyelash glueIn February, researchers tagged more than 14,000 Bogong moths in caves at Mount Kosciuszko. The process was delicate because the insects are small and need to remain capable of flying normally after being released. Some moths were marked with small amounts of non-toxic paint. Others were temporarily sedated with carbon dioxide so researchers could attach tiny paper tags to their wings using eyelash glue. The procedure was designed to allow scientists to identify individual moths if they were encountered later during their migration.The researchers then recruited citizen scientists to help locate the marked insects. Fifty specially designed light traps were installed around the mountains. The traps attract moths at night and hold them safely so volunteers can check them for identifying marks before releasing them. But despite the effort, the result has been surprising: none of the more than 14,000 tagged moths has been found again. For volunteers, the search has meant checking moths regularly and looking closely for the tiny markings. One participant, Kristi Bryant, compared finding a tagged moth to discovering a “golden ticket” because of how rare the marked insects have proved to be, according to ABC News.Missing moths offer cluesAt first, failing to find even one tagged moth might sound like a major setback. Researchers, however, believe the result could contain an unexpected positive message. Eleanor Drinkwater, an entomologist with Invertebrates Australia, explained that the likelihood of finding a tagged individual depends partly on the size of the wider population. If there are more Bogong moths than scientists currently estimate, locating one particular tagged insect becomes much more difficult.Another possibility is that the moths are taking migration routes that do not pass through the monitoring sites. In other words, the missing tags could reveal that scientists still have more to learn about how the insects move across the landscape. The project has also produced useful information even without recovering a single tagged moth. iNaturalist data show a significant increase in untagged Bogong moth sightings, with more than 2,700 recorded in the past year. Researchers plan to use these observations to create heat maps showing where the moths are appearing across the alpine landscape. They will also compare the observations with weather patterns to investigate whether environmental conditions influence the insects' movements.The search continuesResearchers hope to expand the monitoring programme from 50 light traps to as many as 150 next year. The additional traps could provide a wider picture of where Bogong moths are travelling and potentially increase the chances of finding one of the tagged insects. For now, the fate of the 14,000 tagged moths remains a mystery. But their disappearance may offer scientists an unexpected clue: the endangered insects could be more widespread than previously believed, or they may simply be travelling along routes that researchers have yet to discover.Either way, the project is providing researchers with valuable information about a species whose movements remain surprisingly difficult to track. Understanding those movements could ultimately help scientists better protect Bogong moths and the ecosystems that depend on them.

articles.title: South Korea is making AI credits free for every citizen
articles.summary: South Korea plans to hand every citizen free AI access, with no token limits under a program called “AI for All.” No national government has treated advanced...
articles.body:
South Korea plans to hand every citizen free AI access, with no token limits under a program called "AI for All." No national government has treated advanced AI model access as a public service before.

South Korea's Ministry of Science and ICT named three consortia to run the program. They include the country's two biggest telecom operators, along with the company behind Kakao, the app that functions as a general-purpose tool across Korean life.

Each will build its own dedicated app and fold the AI into products people already use.

The state is supplying the chips. Up to 512 Nvidia B200s, split three ways, with the government also covering part of the running costs. What it all adds up to isn't clear, since the Ministry of Science and ICT hasn't attached a number to it. A beta opens in September, with the full rollout later this year.

The AI will plug directly into government systems, letting users book doctors' appointments, look for apartments, and get tax advice. Small businesses, meanwhile, could use it to calculate their taxes and check whether they qualify for state support. Parents, too, can benefit from the program by receiving suggested learning material for their kids.

Right now, foreign AI models run the show. Two-thirds of South Koreans have already tried AI. Ministry tender documents show ChatGPT with 23.45 million Korean users in April, Gemini with 8.45 million, and Claude with 2.41 million. Only around 1.8 million people in the country pay for any of it.

The new quotas, the requirement that most traffic must run on local technology, are designed to change that. Half of every operator's queries have to run through its own certified Korean foundation model, and another 30% through models built by other Korean firms. Eighty percent domestic, in other words.

Foreign models are allowed where the ministry decides they're needed, but without subsidy.

Nobody else has approached AI this way. Brussels set up InvestAI in February 2025 to mobilize €200 billion across the bloc, with €20 billion aimed at compute sites. New Delhi approved its IndiaAI back in March 2024 for roughly $1.25 billion, putting cheap GPUs in front of startups and funding 20 homegrown models.

Both of these have to do with building machinery. Seoul, meanwhile, is handing out the finished product to its citizens.

President Lee Jae-myung's administration has budgeted 10 trillion won for AI in 2026, three times what it spent last year to underwrite the free service.

articles.title: g1 20 anos: da universidade pública à pesquisa com o Hubble, a trajetória da astrônoma brasileira Duília de Mello | G1
articles.standfirst: Pesquisadora participou de estudos sobre a formação de estrelas e galáxias e descobriu uma supernova. Agora, volta à pesquisa para analisar dados do James Webb.
articles.summary: Pesquisadora participou de estudos sobre a formação de estrelas e galáxias e descobriu uma supernova. Agora, volta à pesquisa para analisar dados do James Webb.
articles.body:
Quando o g1 nasceu, há quase 20 anos, o Telescópio Espacial Hubble já estava em órbita havia mais de uma década. Desde então, novos observatórios passaram a enxergar regiões cada vez mais distantes do Universo.

Na astronomia, essa distância também significa olhar para trás no tempo: a luz de estrelas e galáxias muito distantes pode levar bilhões de anos para chegar até a Terra.

“Telescópios são máquinas do tempo, porque conseguem ver bem a fundo, bem profundo. A gente vê objetos bem distantes, e a luz demora para chegar aqui. Então, quando chega, a gente está vendo o passado”, explica a astrônoma brasileira Duília de Mello.

Foi investigando esse passado que Duília construiu boa parte da carreira .

Ela participou de projetos ligados ao Hubble e de pesquisas sobre como estrelas e galáxias surgem e mudam ao longo de bilhões de anos.

Mas a sua trajetória começou bem antes disso, no Rio de Janeiro. Ainda criança, Duília gostava de ficção científica , olhava para o céu e fazia perguntas sobre o espaço. Na época, antes da internet, encontrar respostas não era tão simples.

“Foi aquela curiosidade de criança que me despertou uma grande vontade de entender mais e de estudar a fundo para virar aquela pessoa que entende para explicar aos outros”, conta.

A astrônoma brasileira Duília de Mello durante apresentação na Universidade Católica da América, em Washington, nos Estados Unidos. — Foto: João Pedro de Mello Domingues/Wikimedia Commons

A família não tinha ligação com astronomia. O pai não havia concluído o antigo ginásio e preferia que ela seguisse uma profissão mais tradicional. A mãe queria que os filhos estudassem, mas também se preocupava com o futuro profissional da filha.

Quando Duília tinha cerca de 16 anos, as duas pegaram um ônibus no subúrbio do Rio para conhecer o Observatório do Valongo , da Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ). A visita acabou reforçando a decisão.

“Eu me enxergava um dia professora da UFRJ. Falei para a minha mãe: ‘Eu vou virar uma professora da UFRJ’. Era essa a ideia”, lembra.

Duília cursou Astronomia na UFRJ, fez mestrado no Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas Espaciais (Inpe) e doutorado na Universidade de São Paulo (USP).

Ela diz que as bolsas de estudo foram decisivas para conseguir seguir na carreira. Ainda na graduação, uma bolsa de iniciação científica ajudou inclusive a pagar seu primeiro curso de inglês. Depois vieram bolsas de mestrado, doutorado e pós-doutorado.

“Eu sou muito grata pelo ensino público brasileiro. Tudo que eu sei da vida eu aprendi na UFRJ, no Inpe e na USP”, afirma.

As “bolhas azuis”, grupos de estrelas jovens identificados pelo telescópio Hubble entre as galáxias M81, M82 e NGC 3077, a cerca de 12 milhões de anos-luz da Terra. — Foto: NASA/ESA/HST/STScI/Wikimedia

Em 1997, durante observações no Chile, Duília fez uma das descobertas mais marcantes de sua trajetória: identificou a supernova 1997D , resultado da explosão de uma estrela.

Para ela, o episódio teve um peso que foi além da publicação científica.

“Tinha virado rotina ser astrônoma para mim. Isso é ruim, porque, quando vira rotina, perde o encantamento. Quando descobri a supernova, notei que era realmente esse sentimento, esse processo da descoberta, que tinha me levado a ser astrônoma”, conta.

Anos depois, ela também participou da descoberta das chamadas “ bolhas azuis ”, grupos de estrelas jovens encontrados fora de galáxias, em regiões onde os astrônomos não esperavam encontrar formação estelar.

Outro trabalho envolveu a NGC 6872 , apelidada de Galáxia do Condor. A galáxia espiral chamou atenção pelo tamanho: segundo Duília, as medições indicaram uma extensão equivalente a cerca de cinco vezes a da Via Láctea.

Esses trabalhos fazem parte de uma mesma linha de pesquisa: entender como as galáxias se formam, como interagem umas com as outras e como os elementos químicos se espalham pelo Universo.

Duília explica que esse processo também ajuda a investigar uma pergunta mais próxima de nós: como surgiram os elementos que, bilhões de anos depois, permitiram a formação de planetas como a Terra.

Localização da Supernova 1997D, descoberta por Duília de Mello em 1997 durante observações no Chile. — Foto: Reprodução

Depois de passar anos dividindo a pesquisa com cargos de gestão acadêmica nos Estados Unidos, Duília está voltando a se dedicar integralmente à astronomia.

Um dos seus próximos projetos vai usar dados do Telescópio Espacial James Webb para estudar galáxias observadas quando o Universo ainda era muito mais jovem. A ideia é analisar como a composição química dessas estruturas mudou ao longo de bilhões de anos.

Apesar dos avanços de telescópios como Hubble e Webb, algumas das perguntas mais importantes da astronomia continuam abertas.

Duília cita a matéria escura e a energia escura entre os principais enigmas. A ciência consegue observar seus efeitos no Universo, mas ainda não sabe exatamente do que são feitas.

“Falta muita coisa. Acho que os enigmas mesmo são matéria escura e energia escura. A energia escura parece ser o maior componente do Universo, e a gente não tem a mínima ideia do que é feito”, afirma.

Outra pergunta permanece sem resposta: existe vida fora da Terra?

Duília acredita que a ciência pode estar perto de encontrar planetas com condições compatíveis com a existência de vida, mas ressalta que isso é diferente de encontrar organismos ou estabelecer contato com seres extraterrestres.

“Acho que a gente está prestes a encontrar [sinais da] possibilidade de vida. Mas uma coisa é encontrar possibilidade de vida e outra coisa é ter contato com vida extraterrestre”, diz.

Hoje, ela continua trabalhando justamente em algumas dessas questões, agora com instrumentos capazes de observar regiões do Universo que eram inacessíveis quando iniciou a carreira.

Para Duília, ainda há muito a descobrir — das primeiras galáxias à natureza da matéria e da energia escuras, passando pela busca por outros mundos que possam reunir condições para a vida.
