articles.title: All known life uses 4 DNA letters; UC San Diego showed an existing bacterial enzyme can accurately read and transcribe 8, doubling the genetic alphabet with synthetic letters
articles.summary: Experiments & Discoveries News: All life on Earth, from bacteria to blue whales, writes its genetic instructions using the same four-letter alphabet. These four DNA bases, usually re.
articles.body: All life on Earth, from bacteria to blue whales, writes its genetic instructions using the same four-letter alphabet. These four DNA bases, usually referred to as A, T, C and G, pair up in predictable ways to store and pass on the information needed for life. Now, researchers at UC San Diego have taken a bold step beyond that universal code. In new experiments, they showed that an existing bacterial enzyme can accurately read and transcribe DNA that includes four additional, synthetic letters, effectively doubling the genetic alphabet. As reported by ScienceDaily, the work shows that the machinery of life can be expanded in the lab without redesigning enzymes from scratch, opening fresh possibilities for synthetic biology, medicine and our understanding of what life could be.The natural four letter codeThe story of life as we know it is written in a language of just four chemical characters. In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine, and cytosine pairs with guanine, forming the rungs of the double helix. When a cell divides, these base pairs are copied with amazing fidelity allowing organisms to pass on their genetic information to the next generation. The sequence of these bases determines what proteins a cell makes and proteins perform nearly all functions in the body. This four letter system is so highly conserved that it is found in every known organism. It is one of the strongest pieces of evidence for a common origin of life on Earth. For decades, scientists have wondered if this code is a fundamental requirement for biology or just a historical accident that became fixed early on in evolution .If the genetic alphabet could be expanded, it would suggest that life might be possible with a richer set of instructions than nature has so far used.Adding new letters to the alphabetIn recent years, chemists have designed synthetic DNA bases that can sit alongside the natural four and form stable pairs with each other. These extra letters, often referred to as X and Y in simplified descriptions, have different shapes and chemical properties than A, T, C and G, but they can still fit into the DNA double helix. When incorporated into DNA strands, they create the potential for new codons, the three letter units that specify amino acids during protein synthesis. The challenge has not been just making these synthetic bases, but getting the cell’s own machinery to treat them as legitimate parts of the genetic code. DNA must be copied by enzymes called polymerases, and the resulting RNA must be read by other molecular machines to build proteins. If these enzymes stumble over the new letters, errors creep in and the system breaks down. Early experiments showed that some engineered polymerases could handle expanded alphabets, but they often required substantial redesign and still struggled with accuracy.A bacterial enzyme that already knows howThe new work from UC San Diego adds a surprising twist. Instead of engineering a brand new enzyme to handle eight letter DNA, the researchers tested an existing bacterial enzyme that had never been exposed to synthetic bases before. They found that this naturally occurring polymerase could accurately read DNA containing both the natural four letters and the four synthetic additions, and could transcribe that information into RNA with high fidelity.This result is significant because it suggests that the ability to work with an expanded genetic alphabet may not require completely new molecular inventions. The enzyme’s active site, the region where DNA is read and copied, appears flexible enough to accommodate the extra letters without losing accuracy. Essentially the enzyme treats the synthetic bases as if they were just more letters in the same language, copying them alongside A, T, C and G without confusion. Experiments were done under controlled laboratory conditions, with purified enzymes and well-defined DNA templates. This is very far from a living organism on eight letter DNA, but it is a crucial proof of principle. It shows that at least one key step in the flow of genetic information can work with a doubled alphabet using machinery that already exists in nature.Why doubling the alphabet mattersExpanding DNA's alphabet from four letters to eight massively increases what the genetic code can store. Four letters give nature 64 three-letter combinations, which easily handles our 20 standard amino acids. Jump to eight letters, and those options skyrocket into the hundreds. That extra headroom enables investigators to program cells to make brand new proteins stuffed with custom amino acids. The end result could be targeted medicines, specialized industrial enzymes, or novel materials built from scratch, as well as cleaner genetic circuits that run without messing up normal cellular processes.On a deeper level, this redefines the boundaries of biology. If a natural enzyme can handle eight letters, our four-letter genetic code is not a strict chemical rule. It might just be an evolutionary coin toss. That opens up thrilling possibilities: alien life could operate on a totally different alphabet, or early organisms on Earth may have tested other letters long before settling on the system we have today.Implications for synthetic biology and medicineUsing standard enzymes instead of fragile, re-engineered ones clears a massive hurdle for synthetic biology. Researchers can skip unpredictable lab-built tools and stick with biological machinery they already understand. That shortcut makes it far easier to engineer cells that naturally handle synthetic genetic codes.In medicine, an eight-letter alphabet opens up clever new possibilities. The scientists could design therapeutic genes that bypass a cell’s natural defenses without unwanted side effects. Other letters also make perfect molecular tags for tracking living cells or upgrading diagnostic tests. Beyond health, it boosts digital data storage. DNA is already an incredibly compact archiving medium, but doubling its alphabet packs vastly more information into every single strand.Cautions and open questionsGetting one enzyme to handle an expanded code is just the first hurdle. For a cell to actually survive and function with synthetic DNA, the rest of its internal machinery has to cooperate. It needs to copy the new code, repair damage, and build proteins without glitches. Other essential enzymes might not be nearly as forgiving as the single polymerase tested here. There are real safety risks too. If engineered organisms ever escaped or swapped genetic material with wild species, the results could be completely unpredictable. Scientists will need bulletproof containment strategies and serious safety checks before taking this out of test tubes and into living systems.A broader view of life’s possibilitiesThis UC San Diego discovery challenges standard thinking about DNA. Life's four-letter genetic code isn't an unbendable rule; it is just one setup that happens to work. By proving a natural enzyme can process eight letters, researchers blurred the line between natural and lab-made biology. The machinery for an expanded genetic toolkit was hiding inside living cells all along. For now, it remains early-stage science. But showing that life’s molecular language can grow without starting from square one is massive. As techniques improve, organisms running on expanded alphabets could easily move from a fascinating lab experiment into practical biotech tools.

articles.title: Scientists sent a robot two miles below California and found a bigfin squid; it was the first live Northeast Pacific sighting
articles.summary: Science News: Two miles below the surface of the Pacific Ocean, off the coast of California, in a world of near total darkness and crushing pressure, a remotely ope.
articles.body: Two miles below the surface of the Pacific Ocean, off the coast of California, in a world of near total darkness and crushing pressure, a remotely operated vehicle glided silently through the water. Its cameras were scanning the deep for the strange and the seldom-seen when something extraordinary appeared on its screen. Long trailing arms and a ghostly body drifted into view: a bigfin squid, a species rarely seen alive. For the research team on the ship above, it was a moment of pure wonder. It was the first confirmed live sighting of a bigfin squid in the North-east Pacific, the Los Angeles Times reported, and gave scientists a rare glimpse of one of the ocean’s most elusive inhabitants. Read on to know more:Plunge into the depthsThe expedition was conducted in deep waters off the Central California coast, a region well known for its abundance of marine life and dramatic undersea topography. The research vessel lowered a remotely operated vehicle, or ROV, a robotic submersible piloted from the ship through a long tether. The ROV carries high-definition cameras, lights, and sampling tools that allow it to explore much deeper than a human diver could reach.As the ROV fell through the water column this time, it moved through the transition from where sunlight begins to disappear, then to where it disappears completely. At around two miles down, in the cold, dark expanse of the deep sea, the pilots were searching for organisms that live in this extreme environment. They expected to see strange fish, gelatinous creatures and perhaps a few unusual invertebrates. What they did not expect was to encounter one of the ocean's most mysterious squids.The moment the bigfin appearedAs the ROV moved along a deep slope, the camera picked up a faint shape in the distance. It was difficult to see at first, a pale thing with long, thin tentacles trailing behind it. As the car got closer and its lights came on, details became visible. The thing was thin and long, and its arms and tentacles were of extraordinary length, trailing behind it to a most fantastic extent.For the scientists and pilots monitoring the feed, the sight was both startling and mesmerising. Bigfin squids, members of the genus Magnapinna, are known mostly from a handful of video clips and a few damaged specimens recovered from fishing nets or washed ashore. Most of those records come from other parts of the world, such as the Atlantic, Indian and western Pacific Oceans. To see one alive, and to do so in the Northeast Pacific, was unprecedented.What makes the bigfin squid so unusualBigfin squids stand out even among deep-sea cephalopods. Their most striking feature is their extremely long, thin arms and tentacles, which can be many times their body length. In other footage from other oceans, these limbs hang almost vertically in the water, creating a spooky, curtain-like effect. Scientists aren’t sure what the long tentacles are for, but they believe they may help the squid to sense or catch food in the deep, food-scarce waters.Their bodies are relatively small compared to the span of their arms, and they tend to drift or hover in the water column rather than swim actively. This slow, drifting behaviour, combined with their ghostly appearance, has earned them nicknames like “spooky squid” or “long arm squid” in popular accounts. Because they live so deep and are so fragile, they are rarely encountered intact, and rarely observed alive in their natural habitat.Why this sighting mattersThe Northeast Pacific is one of the most studied ocean regions in the world, yet it still holds major surprises. Many deep sea species have never been seen alive, and some are known only from fragments. Each new live observation adds crucial information about where species live, how they behave and how they fit into the broader ecosystem.This observation of a bigfin broadens the known distribution of the genus into California waters and suggests that these squids are more common than previously thought. It also provides researchers with high quality video to study posture, movement and interaction with the surrounding environment in detail. Observations made over time like this help build up a clearer picture of deep-sea biodiversity and the adaptations that allow life to thrive under extreme conditions.The technology that made it possibleNone of this happens without modern deep-sea robotics. The team relied on a remote sub built to handle crushing pressures miles beneath the surface while broadcasting crisp, real-time video. Soft lighting was engineered to light the pitch-black water just enough to show sharp details without scaring the local wildlife.When a rare bigfin squid drifted into view, shipboard pilots carefully manoeuvred the craft to hold steady rather than chase it. It was a gentle, non-intrusive way of getting amazing images for researchers without stressing the animal, showing why low-impact technology is so important when studying delicate deep-ocean ecology.A moment of wonder for the teamFor the crew on board, this was far more than just a data point. It was pure, spellbinding awe. Deep-sea research sits right at the intersection of hard science and childlike wonder, and this moment hit both notes. The pilots admitted they got so glued to their screens that they forgot they were steering a robot two miles beneath the surface.Moments like this explain why deep-ocean exploration still grips our imagination. Even in a world mapped by satellites, the deep sea remains largely pitch black and uncharted. Each dive is a thrill of discovery, a reminder of how much of our own planet is still hidden in the dark.What is nextResearchers are now going through the footage frame by frame, matching it up with global sightings to try and nail down the exact species, or to see if it’s a unique regional population. They'll also share the video with marine scientists everywhere to help build a clearer picture of deep-ocean life.Beyond the science, clips like this bring a strange, hidden world directly into living rooms and classrooms. To see these creatures in the flesh makes a place most people will never visit feel real. That personal connection is important to galvanising public support for protecting vulnerable ocean habitats from deep-sea mining, aggressive fishing and climate change.A reminder of the ocean’s mysteriesThe bigfin squid did not set out to make history. It was simply living its life in the dark, drifting through water that humans have only begun to explore. Yet its brief appearance on camera reminds us how much of the ocean remains a frontier. New species, new behaviours and new ecosystems are still being discovered, often in places we once thought we understood.For the scientists who witnessed it, the sighting will be a highlight of their careers. For the rest of us, it is an invitation to imagine what else might be out there, waiting in the deep, just beyond the reach of our lights.What are your views on this? Tell us in the comments section below.

articles.title: Japanese students began testing a natural system on a school pond plagued by algae; the experiment eliminated the outbreaks and later expanded to 8 sites
articles.summary: Experiments & Discoveries News: Japanese students at Nakui Agricultural High School in Aomori Prefecture developed a natural water-cleaning system after years of research, and tested.
articles.body: Japanese students at Nakui Agricultural High School in Aomori Prefecture developed a natural water-cleaning system after years of research, and tested it on a pond where recurring algae outbreaks had caused unpleasant smells. According to Japan for Sustainability(JFS), the experiment worked. The pond’s algae outbreaks were completely eliminated, and the system was subsequently installed at eight locations. Known as the ‘Bio-Engine,’ the approach brings together flowering plants, bacteria and fungi instead of relying on conventional machinery and energy. The project later attracted attention not only for cleaning water but also for transforming ponds into colourful spaces filled with flowers. The Nakui Agricultural High school’s environmental research group describes the system as water purification powered by plants and microorganisms, reflecting the idea behind its name. What began as a student research effort became a practical experiment with a wider environmental purpose.Japanese students’ project combined water purification with flowering plants to eliminate algae outbreaksThe project was developed by ‘Team Flora Photonics’ at Nakui Agricultural High School, where students in the environmental research group explored ways to address water pollution. According to JFS, excessive nitrogen and phosphoric acid from household and industrial wastewater can enter lakes and reservoirs, encouraging the growth of algae and causing problems for affected water bodies. The students spent 5 years researching and testing an alternative approach to conventional water-treatment methods. They developed the ‘Bio-Engine,’ a system that relied on ‘SunPatiens plants,’ nitrifying bacteria and mycorrhizal fungi. In 2016, the team tested the system at a pond on the grounds of a local junior high school. The pond had repeatedly experienced algae outbreaks and unpleasant smells. JFS reported that the trial eliminated the outbreaks completely.Despite its name, the Bio-Engine was not a conventional machine. It was designed to clean water through the interaction of living organisms without relying on an external energy supply. As per the school's environmental research group, the SunPatiens flowers were provided through the cooperation of seed company ‘Sakata Seed.’ The flowers were installed in a pond at a local park as part of the group's water-purification work. The flowers also gave the project a distinctive visual character, turning water treatment into something that could also enhance the appearance of a pond. The students even compared their invention with engines made by major automobile manufacturers. This comparison highlighted the system's unique appeal that ‘it performed an environmental function while incorporating living flowers.’The water-treatment experiment expanded to eight sitesThe successful pond trial was followed by the wider use of the Bio-Engine. According to JFS, the water-treatment system was eventually established at 8 locations. The project also received national recognition in 2017, when ‘Team Flora Photonics’ won the Grand Prize in a competition organised by the Faculty of Environmental Studies at Tokyo City University. The students had applied the system at ponds in places including a ‘town hall’ and a ‘library,’ while also carrying out environmental education activities. Judges recognised the group's ambition to develop the system further and explore the possibility of commercialisation, potentially allowing the idea to be used more widely.The project became an essential part of the school's environmental research historyAccording to the school’s official blog, Bio-Engine remains an important part of the school's research history. The combination of visible flowers and biological water treatment had helped make the project stand out. The story of this project offers a clear example of how student research can move beyond a school experiment. From the successful elimination of algae outbreaks to the installation of the system at eight locations, the Bio-Engine demonstrated a practical approach to improving water environments.

articles.title: In 2018, Japan opened a floating solar farm with more than 50,000 panels; 18 months later, Typhoon Faxai's 120mph winds tore modules loose and around 50 panels caught fire
articles.summary: Experiments & Discoveries News: Japan’s push to generate renewable electricity from reservoirs took a dramatic turn in 2019 when a powerful typhoon damaged one of the country’s large.
articles.body: Japan’s push to generate renewable electricity from reservoirs took a dramatic turn in 2019 when a powerful typhoon damaged one of the country’s largest floating solar farms. The project at Yamakura Dam in Ichihara, Chiba Prefecture, began operating in March 2018 with thousands of solar panels spread across the reservoir. According to Kyocera, a Japanese technology and electronics company involved in the project, the 13.7-megawatt plant had 50,904 solar modules installed across about 180,000 square metres of the reservoir. Just 18 months later, Typhoon Faxai brought extremely strong winds to the region, tearing sections of the floating array apart. Some of the displaced panels piled onto other modules, eventually contributing to a fire that involved about 50 panels. The incident highlighted an unusual challenge facing floating solar technology: while placing solar panels on reservoirs can save valuable land, the installations must also withstand powerful winds and the forces created when large floating structures move across water.Japan’s giant floating solar projectAccording to pv magazine, the 13.7-megawatt Yamakura Dam project was damaged when Typhoon Faxai struck the Chiba area with winds reported at about 120 mph. Several solar modules were torn loose and became stacked together, while firefighters said the resulting concentration of heat may have caused the fire. The blaze involved around 50 panels. The plant covered about 44 acres of water and contained 50,904 solar modules supplied by Kyocera.The project had been inaugurated in March 2018 by Kyocera TCL Solar, a joint venture between Kyocera and Tokyo Century. At the time, it was described as Japan’s largest floating solar plant by output. The array occupied approximately 180,000 square metres of the Yamakura Dam reservoir and had an estimated annual generation of 16,170 megawatt-hours, enough to supply electricity equivalent to the consumption of about 4,970 households. The project was built on a reservoir used for industrial water rather than on agricultural or urban land. That was an important reason for choosing floating solar. Japan has limited suitable land for large-scale solar installations, making reservoirs and dams an attractive alternative for renewable-energy projects.When Typhoon Faxai struckThe situation changed dramatically in September 2019. Typhoon Faxai moved through the Chiba region with exceptionally strong winds. The storm was among the strongest to affect the Tokyo region in years, with wind gusts at a nearby Chiba weather station reaching about 207 km/h, or roughly 129 mph. At Yamakura Dam, the wind was strong enough to pull parts of the floating solar array away from their moorings. According to the initial report from pv magazine, several modules were blown loose and stacked on top of other panels. The firefighters investigating the incident said the contact and heat generated by the panels could have created the conditions for the fire. Around 50 modules were reportedly involved in the blaze. The damage, however, went far beyond the visible fire. A later investigation found that a substantial portion of the floating array had been destroyed.Why the panels came looseA subsequent investigation by Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) identified anchor failure as the main cause of the accident, according to pv magazine. The floating island was secured by 420 anchors connected to 823 mooring lines. During the typhoon, seven anchors on the central southern side came loose. Once those anchors failed, the wind loads were distributed unevenly across the remaining structure. This caused resin bolts to fail sequentially, creating a chain reaction that eventually ripped the floating array into three sections. The investigation also identified the size and shape of the floating island and the safety factors used during construction as contributing factors. The incident therefore became more than a single weather-related accident; it provided engineers with information about how large floating solar installations respond to extreme wind conditions.Rebuilding the solar farmThe damaged project was not simply abandoned. Reconstruction began after the incident, with the floating-solar specialist Ciel & Terre and Kyocera working on a redesigned configuration. Instead of recreating the original large, complex floating island, the rebuilt section was divided into smaller square-shaped islands. The change was intended to reduce stress concentration and increase safety factors during extreme weather. By October 2021, Renewables Now reported that Kyocera had restored the roughly 14 MW floating solar park. The restoration demonstrated that the project could return to operation after suffering extensive typhoon damage.A lesson for floating solarThe Yamakura Dam incident illustrates both the promise and vulnerability of floating solar power. Putting solar panels on reservoirs can make use of water surfaces that would otherwise remain unused while avoiding competition for valuable land. The original project was expected to generate more than 16,000 MWh of electricity annually. But floating arrays also face a different set of engineering challenges compared to ground-mounted solar farms. Strong winds can create uplift and movement across the water, placing enormous loads on anchors, mooring systems and floating structures.For Yamakura Dam, Typhoon Faxai exposed those weaknesses only 18 months after the plant began operating. The subsequent redesign turned the damaged facility into a case study in how floating solar systems can be adapted for extreme weather. What began as a showcase for renewable energy ultimately demonstrated another important requirement for the technology: solar panels on water must be designed not only to capture sunlight, but also to survive the storms that move across it.

articles.title: Stoke Space raises another billion to rival SpaceX at re-flying rockets | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Stoke has "completed the initial closing" of a $1B Series E round intended to help it reach orbit and prepare a new, larger rocket for operations.
articles.body:
The fuel for a fully reusable rocket that can unlock truly low-cost access to space isn’t methane or liquid oxygen. It’s cash, and Stoke Space Technologies is tanking up. The company has now “completed the initial closing” of a $1 billion Series E round intended to help it reach orbit and prepare a new, larger rocket for operations.

“This round is really to scale,” CEO Andy Lapsa told TechCrunch. “To lay the infrastructure, to scale in production and flight frequency, and importantly to fund the development of the second generation vehicle.”

The round was led by Point72 Ventures (hedge fund billionaire Steve Cohen’s tech investment vehicle), and Spark Capital, and included investment from General Innovation, Glade Brook Capital, US Innovation Technology, Washington Harbour Partners, Woven Capital and Y Combinator, among others.

Stoke is one of a handful of startups attempting to compete with Elon Musk’s SpaceX in the low-cost rocket launch space. SpaceX was built around the Falcon 9, which has a reusable booster stage, and now Musk and company are trying to field a huge, fully-reusable rocket, Starship.

But unlike its rivals Rocket Lab, Relativity Space or Firefly Aerospace, Lapsa’s company is aiming straight at that holy grail: A rocket where both the booster stage and the payload-carrying second stage come back to Earth so they can be reused cheaply. It’s never been done before.

Such ambition and technical feats require capital. SpaceX has spent well over $10 billion on Starship over the last decade, and the vehicle still hasn’t yet reached orbit, although that may change on its next flight. Now, Stoke has raised $2.3 billion in total.

In particular, SpaceX has struggled to identify the right materials and configuration for the components that shield the second stage of the rocket from the extreme heat caused when it is reentering the atmosphere. Stoke instead flows super-cooled liquid hydrogen through its thermal shielding, a unique active cooling solution that Lapsa says has been tested exhaustively on the ground and will be deployed on the first flight.

“We can flow excess coolant — more than we think we need in order to overcool the surface of the vehicle — and take a conservative stance from that perspective in early flights,” he said.

Lapsa said that he expects Stoke’s first vehicle, the Nova Pathfinder, to take flight in early 2027. In a business known for delays, he’s confident sharing that target following a series of structural and operational tests on the rocket’s first stage at the company’s Moses Lake facility. Next up is test-firing each stage of the rocket on the ground to ensure they are ready for flight.

“The ground system is checked out to the extent that we can do it without the rocket, and the rocket’s checked out to the extent that we can do it without the launch pad,” Lapsa said. “So the next step is to do them together.”

The startup has already sold launch contracts on the vehicle, which can carry three metric tons to low-Earth orbit — that will be, Lapsa believes, the largest debut vehicle of any U.S. rocket maker. That said, few rockets get off the ground on time or with total success, and simply getting to orbit would be an achievement.

“We have multiple Pathfinder vehicles in production, and we have confidence that we will bring Pathfinder to market and into orbit regardless of this round,” Lapsa said.

Stoke also revealed plans for an even bigger rocket, the Nova Block 2, that has been under development for the past few years. Based on the same technologies as the Pathfinder, including the engines and the company’s novel heat shield, that vehicle will be able to bring 15 metric tons to low-Earth orbit, slightly more than the Falcon 9.

The goal is to deploy it in 2029, right when, according to Musk, the Falcon 9 will be phased out. Is Lapsa drooling at the possibility of picking up increasingly desperate launch customers just as SpaceX pulls back?

“It amplifies the mismatch between launch supply and demand for launch, there’s no question about that,” he admits. “Regardless of Falcon 9 retiring or not retiring, the space industry and the space economy scales exactly as fast as rockets get off the ground, particularly rockets that serve third-party customers.”

That last remark is a dog whistle that satellite operators will surely hear: When SpaceX’s Starship takes flight, companies and government agencies looking to buy tickets will be competing with the space company’s internal projects, and might have to pay a premium to use the big rocket. Stoke, on the other hand, has not revealed plans to operate its own space assets.

“Now is the time to get moving […] so that we can finally start deploying a lot of the constellations and applications that we aspire to as an industry but have been stuck on the ground,” Lapsa said.

articles.body: More than 100 ‘eagle rays’ were recorded gathering around a tuna ranch off the north-eastern coast of Malta. Scientists believe it is the largest aggregation of the species ever recorded. The remarkable sighting was captured during routine underwater monitoring in October 2024, when a remotely operated vehicle surveyed the seabed beneath several tuna cages. Researchers estimated that between 100-150 rays were present, moving through the water and across the seabed where leftover food fish had accumulated. The study, published in the journal ‘Marine Biodiversity,’ suggests that this gathering was largely driven by the opportunity to feed on this readily available food. Common eagle ray aggregations are rarely documented, making the discovery particularly significant. The researchers also noted that the species is considered vulnerable in the Mediterranean, raising important questions about how tuna farming may influence the behaviour and conservation of these rays.How the 100 eagle rays were recorded gathering around the Malta tuna farmThe discovery was made during routine monitoring of the seabed near tuna ranches off Malta. According to the study, researchers surveyed 8 of the 24 tuna cages on the site, along with 4 nearby reference locations. A remotely operated vehicle(ROV), collected video footage at depths of around 50-55 metres. Out of the eight cages surveyed, three had fresh food fish resting on the seabed beneath them.The largest gathering of common eagle rays (Myliobatis aquila), was found around one of these cages. Their constant movement made an exact count difficult, but researchers estimated from the footage that between 100-150 individuals were present. Smaller numbers of other rays, including common stingrays, were also observed. However, this gathering of eagle rays was not like any previously documented for the species. Earlier reports have described much smaller groups, and the researchers believe this Malta sighting is the largest recorded aggregation of common eagle rays till date.Leftover fish created a rare feeding opportunity for the eagle raysThe footage provided a strong clue about what had brought so many rays together. The large aggregations were observed only beneath cages where food fish used to feed the tuna had accumulated on the seabed. Under the remaining cages, where no food fish were present, researchers recorded only isolated rays. The ROV also captured the eagle rays actively feeding on the fish. They frequently bumped into one another while moving around the seabed, and two individuals were seen tugging at the same piece of food. The researchers said these direct observations provide strong evidence that scavenging on leftover fish was a major reason for the aggregation. The study noted that previous observations of common eagle ray gatherings had rarely provided such clear evidence about why the animals had come together.The gathering brought together adults and younger eagle rays of different sizesThe gathering included both large and small individuals. Several eagle rays had an estimated disc width of more than 80 centimetres, while others measured about 20 centimetres, suggesting smaller animals were part of the population. The researchers estimated the rays' size by comparing them with the food fish on the seabed, which were approximately 20 centimetres long. Among the individuals that could be examined closely enough to determine their sex, all appeared to be female because researchers did not observe male reproductive structures known as ‘claspers.’ However, the study did not rule out the presence of males elsewhere in the group. The sighting also occurred during a period that roughly overlaps with the species' breeding season in the west and central Mediterranean. Yet the researchers could not determine whether reproduction played any role in the gathering and concluded that feeding appeared to be the primary explanation.The tuna ranch may be changing the dietary habits of the eagle raysCommon eagle rays mainly feed on ‘molluscs,’ although fish can also form part of their diet. The abundance of food beneath the tuna cages may therefore provide the animals with an easy feeding opportunity. The study suggests that this could temporarily alter their normal feeding behaviour and encourage the rays to remain near the ranches while food is available. During fallow periods, when the farms are not feeding tuna, their diet and behaviour may return to usual patterns typical of the surrounding Maltese waters. The findings illustrate how aquaculture operations can influence nearby wildlife. Food that escapes or falls from fish farms can affect ‘where wild animals gather and obtain part of their diet.’What does the record eagle ray gathering mean for conservationThe discovery has particular conservation significance because the common eagle ray is classified as vulnerable in the Mediterranean. The gathering of such large numbers in one location could create both opportunities and risks. The researchers noted that predictable concentrations could make the rays easier to target by fishers. Although there is no fishery specifically targeting eagle rays in Malta, the species is caught and traded in other parts of the Mediterranean.The study suggested that additional fishing restrictions around the tuna ranches could help protect these aggregations. At the same time, the researchers warned that aquaculture sites can alter the natural movement patterns and behaviour of wild marine animals. Continued monitoring could help determine whether the Malta gathering was an isolated event, a seasonal occurrence or part of a pattern linked to feeding activities at the tuna ranches. The extraordinary sighting has opened a new window into the behaviour of a species whose large gatherings have remained poorly understood.

articles.title: Indian startup Agnikul Cosmos unveils testing & manufacturing hubs in Chennai to validate reusable rocket stages
articles.summary: Science News: NEW DELHI: In a giant step towards attaining reusable launch vehicle technology like Elon Musk's SpaceX, Indian space startup Agnikul Cosmos has inaug.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In a giant step towards attaining reusable launch vehicle technology like Elon Musk's SpaceX, Indian space startup Agnikul Cosmos has inaugurated two new assembly and testing facilities in Chennai.The company unveiled the Stage Testing & Inspection Facility (STIF) and the Pressurant Tank Realisation, Over-wrapping and Outfitting Facility (PROOF) at its assembly and testing facility. The facilities were inaugurated in the presence of Group Captain and Indian astronaut Shubhanshu Shukla.STIF is a fully in-house facility for testing reusable rocket stages under flight-like operating conditions. The facility also supports post-flight inspection and requalification of recovered stages. It supports thrust levels from 1 kN to 200 kN, LOX sub-cooling down to 73 K and full-duration burns of up to 150 seconds. The facility will also be used to inspect and requalify recovered stages after flight.PROOF will enable the in-house manufacturing of pressure vessels — the rocket component that holds gases or liquids at a pressure significantly different from the outside environment. The new facility can produce more than 10 vessels a month, including vessels of up to 3,500 litres and 350 bar.“The vision of bringing reusability to launch requires us to think beyond a single flight and build the capability to test, recover, inspect and prepare a stage for its next flight. STIF gives us the ability to test complete stages for the duration of their mission and inspect and requalify recovered stages. This is an important capability as we work towards Mission-02,” said Srinath Ravichandran, co-founder and CEO, Agnikul Cosmos.Grp Capt and astronaut Shukla said, “India’s space programme is entering an exciting phase, with capabilities being built across the country that will enable increasingly ambitious missions. It is encouraging to see Agnikul continue to expand its capabilities in advanced manufacturing and testing.”Headquartered in Chennai and incubated at IIT Madras, Agnikul Cosmos develops the Agnibaan family of configurable small-lift launch vehicles. In May 2024, it conducted Mission 01, Agnibaan SOrTeD, from its privately built launchpad at Sriharikota.Agnikul already designs and manufactures its single-piece, 3D-printed semi-cryogenic engines in-house and develops its avionics and other propulsion and vehicle systems.

articles.title: A man climbed inside a giant Roman storage jar around 1,600 years ago and never came out; archaeologists think they know what he was hiding from
articles.summary: Archaeology & Ancient World News: More than 1,600 years ago, as violence swept through a Roman settlement in what is now Bulgaria, a man appears to have made a desperate attempt to sur.
articles.body: More than 1,600 years ago, as violence swept through a Roman settlement in what is now Bulgaria, a man appears to have made a desperate attempt to survive. He climbed inside a huge ceramic storage jar and hid there, possibly hoping the vessel would protect him from an attack and the fire spreading through the settlement. He never came out. Archaeologists have now uncovered his skeleton inside the jar at the ancient Roman colony of Deultum, providing an unusually direct glimpse into the final moments of a person caught in a violent episode. The discovery is especially striking because the vessel was not a burial container. It was an everyday storage jar, making the circumstances surrounding the man's death highly unusual. According to a Live Science report, the remains were discovered on August 10, 2026, during excavations of a Late Roman turret near Deultum's western gate. The skeleton, believed to belong to a young man, was found inside a large vessel known as a dolium, along with two iron knives and a belt. Archaeologists believe he may have climbed inside the jar during an enemy attack, possibly seeking shelter after a fire had already started.A giant jar becomes a hiding placeThe vessel in which the man was found was a dolium, a large Roman ceramic container used to store commodities such as wine, olive oil and other goods. These vessels could be enormous, with the largest examples capable of holding more than 1,000 litres. The surviving part of the newly discovered vessel measured about one metre across. Its size would have made it physically possible for a person to climb inside, although using it as a hiding place was certainly not its intended purpose. The discovery was made in a Late Roman turret, or small defensive tower, forming part of Deultum's western gate. Archaeologists were excavating the structure when they unexpectedly encountered human remains.Evidence of a violent attackThe location of the skeleton provides important clues about what may have happened. Archaeologists found extensive evidence of burning around the dolium, including ash and charcoal, broken bricks and roof tiles, blackened walls, melted pieces of glass and animal bones. The area therefore appears to have experienced a destructive event involving fire. Researchers also found numerous bronze coins, which may have been lost during the chaos. The preliminary archaeological evidence dates the event to around A.D. 400, although researchers say a more precise date will be possible after further analysis of the excavation data.What was he hiding from?The exact attack responsible for the destruction remains unknown. However, Deultum experienced repeated attacks during the fourth and fifth centuries, including attacks associated with East Germanic groups and the Huns. According to Live Science, archaeologist Lyudmil Vagalinski of the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences believes the man may have entered the jar when an attack was already underway. One clue is particularly important: archaeologists found ash beneath the skeleton. This suggests that the fire had already begun before the man entered the vessel, rather than the fire starting after he was already hiding inside. The researchers therefore think he may have been attempting to escape the flames or the attackers outside.Two knives with the skeletonThe objects found with the man add another layer to the discovery. He had two iron knives. One was apparently positioned between his legs, while another was associated with his belt. Archaeologist Lyudmil Vagalinski suggested that the knives may have been carried for protection in case attackers discovered his hiding place.However, researchers do not believe the man was necessarily a soldier. The weapons could simply have been personal possessions or tools that he carried when he sought shelter. His position inside the vessel is also significant. According to the archaeological team, the skeleton was positioned much like someone who had been sleeping or crouching. There was no indication that he had attempted to climb back out.A city rebuilt without knowing he was therePerhaps the most remarkable part of the discovery came after the attack. Following the destruction, the inhabitants apparently levelled the ruins of the tower and constructed a new, higher floor over the area. They seemingly did not realise that a person remained inside the large storage vessel below. That meant the man and the circumstances of his death remained hidden for roughly 1,600 years.Human remains are relatively unusual inside ancient urban settlements because people who died during ordinary circumstances were generally collected and buried outside city walls. According to Vagalinski, discoveries such as this can occur when extraordinary events, including attacks, fires, earthquakes or volcanic eruptions, leave victims trapped beneath the destruction.What happens next?The skeleton has now been transferred to Sofia, Bulgaria, where a physical anthropologist will examine the remains. That analysis could provide more information about the man's age, health and possibly the circumstances surrounding his death. Archaeologists also plan to return to Deultum next summer to continue excavating the western Roman gate and investigate the northern turret where the jar was discovered. Their work could help establish a more precise chronology for the destruction. For now, the evidence points to a haunting sequence of events. Around A.D. 400, as violence and fire consumed part of Deultum, a man appears to have climbed into an enormous storage jar in search of safety. With two knives and his belt still with him, he stayed inside but never emerged. His hiding place eventually became an accidental time capsule, preserving the story of a desperate attempt to survive an attack more than 1,600 years ago.

articles.title: Scientists found hidden populations within common gut bacteria that can spread internationally within decades and are associated with ageing, colorectal cancer, IBD and type 2 diabetes
articles.summary: Experiments & Discoveries News: The human gut is home to trillions of microorganisms that together form the gut microbiome. These microbes play important roles in digestion, immune f.
articles.body: The human gut is home to trillions of microorganisms that together form the gut microbiome. These microbes play important roles in digestion, immune function and metabolism. Now, researchers led by the University of Vienna have found that common gut bacteria may be more complex and more transmissible than previously thought.The study found hidden populations within several common bacterial species. Some of these populations were associated with advanced age, colorectal cancer, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and type 2 diabetes. The researchers also found evidence that some bacterial populations can spread between people and across continents, Science Daily reported.In some cases, these bacterial populations appear to have expanded across continents within only a few decades. Such rapid international spread has mainly been observed in pathogens in earlier research. The new findings suggest that ordinary gut bacteria can also move between populations and establish themselves in new environments.The study, published in Nature, could change how scientists study links between the gut microbiome and disease. Instead of looking at an entire bacterial species as one group, researchers may be able to identify smaller populations that have adapted to specific conditions inside the gut.Looking Beyond Bacterial SpeciesMost microbiome studies group bacteria by species or broad genetic similarity. While this approach is useful, it can hide differences between bacterial populations that have adapted to different conditions inside the human gut.As a result, it can be difficult to establish whether a particular bacterium is directly linked to a disease, is simply present at the same time, or could have a protective effect. The University of Vienna team therefore looked for bacterial groups that showed signs of adaptation and specialisation.The researchers used an analytical strategy called “reverse ecology”. This approach uses genomic information to understand how organisms have adapted to particular environments.The team examined thousands of bacterial isolates collected from the human gut, along with large amounts of metagenomic data from people in different countries and from different age and health groups. Metagenomic data contains the complete genetic information of microbial communities found in a sample.Genetic Clues Reveal Hidden PopulationsOne important clue came from what scientists call “genome-wide selective sweeps”. This happens when an individual develops a beneficial mutation that gives it an advantage over closely related individuals.As the successful individual and its descendants become dominant, genetic diversity within that population falls. This can help researchers identify groups that are closely related in ancestry and biological function.Using these signals, the researchers found that many familiar gut bacterial species could actually be divided into several distinct evolutionary lineages. These populations appear to be adapted to different conditions within the gut.“If you don't just count species but take evolutionary adaptation into account, you can identify the biologically relevant units in the microbiome much more accurately,” said lead author Xiaoqian Annie Yu of the Centre for Microbiology and Environmental Systems Science (CeMESS), University of Vienna.“Even within the same bacterial species, some populations occur more frequently than others in certain diseases. When all are considered together, this often remains hidden.”Some Gut Bacteria Can Spread InternationallyThe researchers also found evidence that some particularly competitive bacterial populations can spread over large geographic distances. In some cases, they appear to have expanded across continents within just a few decades.The finding is notable because patterns of such rapid spread have previously been seen mainly among pathogens. The study suggests that gut bacteria that are not necessarily pathogens can also move between people and populations.“Our findings show that gut bacteria are also more dynamic than previously thought. Well-adapted strains can spread internationally and occupy new ecological niches,” said study leader Martin F. Polz of the University of Vienna.The findings also indicate that the composition of the gut microbiome may be influenced by more than diet, medication and lifestyle. Transmission between people could also play a role in determining which bacterial populations become established and spread.Could This Improve Microbiome-Based Treatment?The discovery may help researchers make more precise connections between gut bacteria and disease. Rather than considering every member of a bacterial species in the same way, scientists could focus on specific populations associated with particular health conditions.This could help in the search for more precise microbiome biomarkers. In the longer term, it may also support treatments designed to target specific bacterial populations instead of entire species.Such approaches could potentially encourage beneficial bacterial strains while suppressing populations associated with harmful effects. However, the study does not establish such treatments; it identifies bacterial populations and their associations.The researchers now plan to investigate which genes distinguish these bacterial populations from one another. They also want to understand what biological functions are produced by these genetic differences.

articles.title: In 1980, conservationists began eradicating feral sheep to restore California's Santa Cruz Island; by 1987 numbers fell from 21,500 to under 100, then 12 lambs were rescued to save the breed
articles.summary: Wildlife & Biodiversity News: In 1980, conservationists began an ambitious ecological restoration programme on Santa Cruz Island, off the coast of Southern California. The main goa.
articles.body: In 1980, conservationists began an ambitious ecological restoration programme on Santa Cruz Island, off the coast of Southern California. The main goal was to remove tens of thousands of feral sheep whose uncontrolled grazing was damaging native plants and threatening wildlife habitats. Over the next seven years, organised eradication efforts dramatically changed the island’s landscape. According to historical records from The Livestock Conservancy and information documented in Wikipedia’s Santa Cruz sheep entry, the feral population fell from about 21,500 to fewer than 100 animals by 1987. With a genetically distinct heritage breed close to extinction, conservationists launched a rescue mission, capturing 12 lambs to save the breed on the American mainland.A centuries-long presence on the islandDomestic sheep were first brought to Santa Cruz Island in the mid-19th century. Historical information from Islapedia shows that livestock operations were established around 1851 under Spanish and American ranch managers. For decades, large-scale sheep shearing was an important activity across the island’s rough landscape. But this changed during the 20th century. When private owner Edwin L. Stanton bought the western part of the island in 1937, he shifted the main focus of the ranches to cattle. Sheep shearing stopped across large areas, leaving thousands of sheep without proper management. Over many generations, the animals returned to a completely wild state and adapted to the difficult conditions of the Channel Islands. Cut off from mainland sheep, the Santa Cruz animals developed special traits that helped them survive. They became smaller, very agile, resistant to many common sheep diseases and able to live on limited vegetation without human care. However, their growing population became a serious threat to the island’s already fragile ecosystem.Environmental crisis and eradication effortsBy the late 1970s, the island’s natural plant life was under severe pressure. Large numbers of feral sheep were eating native vegetation, causing soil erosion and destroying habitats needed by endemic species. In 1980, environmental non-profit organisation The Nature Conservancy took control of most of Santa Cruz Island and began a major restoration project. Research by ecologist Dirk Van Vuren, published in the journal Biological Conservation, showed how heavy sheep grazing was damaging trees and stopping native plants from growing back. To restore the island’s natural biodiversity, conservation workers began a large-scale eradication programme. Field teams used controlled hunts and aerial shooting from helicopters to reach remote valleys and ridges. Within seven years, the population of about 21,500 sheep had been reduced to fewer than 100.The rescue of a rare genetic lineageWhile environmentalists welcomed the return of native plants, livestock historians realised that a unique heritage breed was also close to disappearing. Research by The Livestock Conservancy, then known as the American Minor Breeds Conservancy (AMBC), showed that Santa Cruz sheep had a rare and largely unchanged genetic line linked to 19th-century Spanish and Merino sheep. In a feature published in The Livestock Conservancy’s News archive, researchers Phil Hedrick, Marion Stanley and Dirk Van Vuren played important roles in efforts to save the breed. With the last island sheep facing possible extinction, conservationists stepped in late in 1987. A small team captured 12 wild lambs from the remaining flock and moved them across the Santa Barbara Channel to the California mainland. These 12 animals became the foundation of a captive breeding programme created to protect the breed’s future.Securing the breed’s survival off the islandMoving from a wild island environment to mainland farms created new challenges. The rescued lambs were not used to people and needed careful handling by experienced rare-breed owners. With help from private breeders, educational institutions and heritage livestock organisations, the mainland population slowly grew. The Livestock Conservancy introduced strict registration standards to reduce inbreeding while keeping the breed’s genetic line pure. By the late 1990s, further rescue efforts by animal welfare groups such as Farm Sanctuary brought more sheep away from the remaining private parts of the island before government eradication programmes were completed. Today, Santa Cruz sheep remain one of the rarest sheep breeds in North America. The rescue carried out in 1987 ensured that these hardy animals survived in small conservation flocks across the United States. They now serve as a living link to California’s agricultural history and an example of successful livestock conservation.

articles.title: As El Niño intensifies, scientists in Chile are making a vulnerable penguin species wear copper vests to help them heal faster
articles.summary: Wildlife & Biodiversity News: El Niño is wreaking havoc not only on humans and the climate, but also animals. From ferocious tigers to little waddling penguins, everyone has been b.
articles.body: El Niño is wreaking havoc not only on humans and the climate, but also animals. From ferocious tigers to little waddling penguins, everyone has been bearing their souls with the heightening heat that remains undefeated and overpowering. Amidst this, researchers in Chile have designed an unlikely new garment for injured penguins, snug red vests threaded with copper and zinc that they hope will help the aquatic birds heal faster, according to a report by US News & World Report.In the past, veterinarians have tried the same with injured dogs and cats and found success. Now, they are trying out the technology on Humboldt penguins in Chile, home to the largest concentration of the vulnerable species. “For years, vests with microfibers containing elements like copper and zinc have been tested on pets, particularly dogs and cats, and have greatly helped in the recovery of skin wounds,” said Ignacio Idalsoaga, director of the Buin Zoo, a wildlife park on the outskirts of Chile’s capital, Santiago, where researchers took measurements of penguins to develop the first bodysuits.“We began to wonder — why can't this be used on penguins?" he told The Associated Press from the zoo on Wednesday.Saving a declining populationThe experiment comes as Chile's Humboldt penguin population is declining rapidly. Chilean and international researchers surveying the country's major breeding colonies in 2024 and 2025 found a 63% drop in active nests compared to the same sites three years earlier. Chile, the world's top copper producer, is home to 80% of the world's remaining Humboldt penguins, ⁠and scientists at the Universidad de Concepción estimate that their numbers have dwindled to fewer than 20,000 from around 45,000 in the late 1990s.Typically, the birds face mounting threats from entanglement in fishing nets, plastic pollution, disease outbreaks and competition with fisheries for food. Now, they also find themselves in the crosshairs with one of the world's most disruptive weather patterns, El Niño. The pattern brings in unusually warm waters to parts of the Pacific Ocean, making the cold-water fish that they rely on harder to find. This forces the penguin parents to travel farther for food and leave their nests behind.“Especially now, with all the problems caused by El Niño, we’re likely to see many abandoned chicks in the coming weeks, with injuries they suffer in the environment,” Idalsoaga said.Wildlife clinics across Chile have been receiving distressed penguins stranded along the coast, some cut by fishing nets or boat propellers, others weakened by a lack of food, shared Tomas Pino, a veterinarian who runs Conservacion Humboldt, a nonprofit that rehabilitates injured marine animals in the country's north.Treating injuries fasterWhen they get injured, penguins often twist their long necks to peck at the gashes and often end up pulling out their own stitches. The vests made by the researchers prevent them from doing that while putting copper to work as a salve. Copper and zinc woven into the fabric help inhibit the growth of bacteria, fungi and mites. Moreover, zinc also stimulated the formation of new blood vessels, helping damaged tissue heal faster.The suit was created by adapting copper bodysuits ‌previously used on four-legged animals for birds, through a collaboration between the Humboldt Conservation Centre, a non-profit, the Catholic University of the North and textile innovation company Kimba Vet.The suits were tested on five penguins at the Humboldt Conservation Centre in Coquimbo, which rehabilitates two species of penguins on Chile's central rocky coast: Humboldt and Magellanic penguins. Four of the birds had wounds believed to have been caused by human activity, most likely entanglement ⁠in fishing nets.“We’ve seen that the penguins tolerate it quite well,” Pino said. “We noticed that from one day to the next, the wounds were in better condition with the vest."

articles.title: Unblinking stare into the void: Why Nasa's Roman telescope is our best bet to find life in the stars
articles.summary: Science News: Imagine pointing a telescope at the crowded heart of the Milky Way and asking it to keep watching, not for hours or days, but for years. Every tiny fl.
articles.body: Imagine pointing a telescope at the crowded heart of the Milky Way and asking it to keep watching, not for hours or days, but for years. Every tiny flicker, movement or change in the light of hundreds of millions of stars could potentially tell astronomers that something is there: a new planet, a wandering world, a distant black hole or perhaps an Earth-like planet hidden among the stars.That is the promise of Nasa’s newest space observatory, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.Roman was launched on August 30 aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from Nasa’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The telescope is now on its journey to its destination nearly 1 million miles from Earth, where it will spend years surveying the universe.And there is already plenty of excitement around it. During a post-launch press conference, Nasa official Jared Isaacman received a phone call from US President Donald Trump, who was reportedly enthusiastic about the mission.“The president’s excited about Roman,” Isaacman said before putting Trump on speaker. Trump congratulated the team and remarked that the launch had looked beautiful on television.But what exactly is Roman going to do? And the question that is likely to grab the most attention: could this telescope actually find aliens?The short answer is: it could help scientists find planets that might be capable of supporting life, but it is not designed to directly discover little green men, or even alien microbes.Here is why Roman could nevertheless become a major step in the search for life beyond Earth.So, what is Roman Space Telescope?Named after Nancy Grace Roman, Nasa’s first chief astronomer, the Roman Space Telescope is a new-generation observatory designed to study some of the biggest mysteries in the universe.Its targets include dark energy, the mysterious phenomenon associated with the accelerating expansion of the universe; distant galaxies; stars; and, importantly, exoplanets — planets orbiting stars beyond our Sun.Roman is not simply a replacement for the Hubble Space Telescope or the James Webb Space Telescope.Think of the three as having different jobs.Hubble is famous for producing extraordinarily detailed images of individual cosmic objects and studying the universe in ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light.James Webb, meanwhile, is particularly powerful for looking at very distant and ancient objects in infrared wavelengths. It effectively gives astronomers a highly sensitive zoom lens into deep space.Roman brings something different, a panoramic view.Instead of concentrating on one small patch of the sky at a time, Roman can survey enormous areas and detect changes across them. Its observations can then help astronomers identify objects that Hubble or Webb can examine in much greater detail.In other words, if Hubble and Webb are cosmic photographers with powerful zoom lenses, Roman is more like a giant wide-angle camera scanning the sky for anything interesting.Why is Milky Way so important?One of Roman's most fascinating assignments will take it into the heart of our own galaxy.More than a quarter of its planned five-year primary mission will be devoted to repeatedly observing the galactic bulge — the densely packed central region of the Milky Way.This region is roughly 10,000 light-years wide and contains an enormous number of stars. It is so crowded that previous telescopes have struggled to study its depths.Roman will repeatedly photograph a relatively narrow section of this region, recording an image approximately every 12 minutes during its Galactic Bulge Time-Domain Survey.Why keep looking at same stars again and again?Because the universe is constantly changing.Stars brighten and dim. Objects move. Planets pass in front of their stars. And sometimes the gravity of an unseen object causes a distant star to suddenly appear brighter.Roman is designed to catch these fleeting changes.Scientists expect it could monitor hundreds of millions of stars in this relatively small area of the Milky Way.And that huge number is important because some of the events astronomers are looking for are extremely rare.The cosmic trick called gravitational microlensingOne of Roman’s most important planet-hunting tools will be gravitational microlensing.The idea sounds complicated, but the basic principle is surprisingly simple.Imagine a distant star sitting behind another star from our point of view on Earth. The gravity of the closer star bends the light coming from the distant one.As the foreground object moves across our line of sight, the background star can briefly appear brighter.That is gravitational microlensing.Now add a planet.If the foreground star has a planet orbiting it, the planet can create a tiny additional change in the star’s light. Roman can detect that brief signal.This technique is particularly useful because it can detect planets that other methods struggle to find, including relatively small, rocky worlds.It could even help scientists find Earth-sized planets and determine how common such worlds are in our galaxy.There is, however, a catch.A microlensing event is generally a one-time cosmic alignment. Once it is over, astronomers may not get another chance to observe the same planet in the same way.That makes these discoveries incredibly valuable, but sometimes difficult to study further.Roman will also look for planets crossing starsMicrolensing is not Roman’s only trick.The telescope will also search for transits.A transit happens when a planet passes directly in front of its star from our viewpoint. The planet blocks a tiny amount of the star’s light, creating a small dip that astronomers can detect.Unlike microlensing, transits happen repeatedly as a planet completes its orbit.This makes them particularly useful because scientists can observe the same planetary system again and again.Roman’s observations of the galactic bulge are expected to uncover an astonishing number of new worlds. Scientists estimate the survey could identify around 100,000 exoplanets, with its sensitivity potentially extending down to objects as small as the Moon.That could dramatically expand our understanding of how many planets are out there — and what kinds of planetary systems exist.So, can Roman discover aliens?This is where things get really interesting.Roman is not an alien-detection machine. It will not necessarily photograph an alien civilisation or pick up a message from extraterrestrials.What it can do is help answer a question that comes before that:How common are potentially Earth-like worlds?Scientists currently know of more than 6,000 confirmed exoplanets, but there are almost certainly vastly more waiting to be discovered.Roman could help astronomers determine how frequently small, rocky planets form, whether they tend to orbit stars, and where such planets are located.Its coronagraph instrument adds another exciting capability. A coronagraph blocks the overwhelming glare of a star, making it easier to see much fainter objects nearby.Roman’s coronagraph is designed to potentially capture direct images of Jupiter-sized exoplanets around nearby stars.That does not mean it will immediately reveal an alien civilisation. But directly observing planets is an important step towards understanding their atmospheres, environments and potential habitability.The broader search for life will also involve other telescopes and future missions. If Roman identifies particularly interesting worlds, those targets could potentially be studied in greater detail by observatories such as Webb.It isn't just about planetsRoman’s science programme goes far beyond the search for alien worlds.By repeatedly surveying huge numbers of stars, it could uncover previously unknown brown dwarfs, black holes, neutron stars and other unusual objects.It could also help scientists understand the history of the Milky Way itself.The galactic bulge is believed to contain some of the oldest stars in our galaxy. But astronomers still do not have a complete picture of exactly how old those stars are or how the region evolved.Roman could effectively conduct a huge population survey of the galactic centre — revealing not just individual objects but patterns in how stars and planets formed and changed.And beyond our galaxy, Roman will investigate dark energy, one of the biggest unanswered questions in modern cosmology.Dark energy is linked to the observation that the expansion of the universe is accelerating. Understanding it could help scientists explain how the universe evolved and what its ultimate fate might be.When will Roman start working?The launch was only the beginning.After reaching space, Roman began deploying its solar panels, high-gain antenna and large deployable aperture cover, essentially a giant sunshade designed to keep unwanted light from interfering with its observations.The telescope’s Coronagraph Instrument was also powered on in early September. Engineers will spend weeks testing and calibrating it before science operations begin.Roman is targeted to become fully operational around January 2027.And that is when the real cosmic treasure hunt begins.For astronomers, the most exciting possibility may not be one spectacular discovery. It could be the sheer volume of information Roman produces.Hundreds of millions of stars. Tens of thousands of planets. Countless changes in the night sky.Somewhere in all that data could be an entirely new class of planet, an unexpected kind of star or a cosmic object scientists never knew existed.And perhaps, among those distant worlds, Roman may help answer one of humanity’s oldest questions:Will it find aliens?It may not find aliens directly. But by showing us just how many potentially Earth-like worlds are out there, Roman could bring us closer than ever to finding out.

articles.title: Around 1,800 years ago, a Roman household decorated its floor with a cat named 'Emerald' and a dog named 'Ocean'; archaeologists have now uncovered the mosaic
articles.summary: Archaeology & Ancient World News: Around 1,800 years ago, a Roman household in what is now Turkey decorated the floor of its home with a detailed mosaic showing animals and mythologica.
articles.body: Around 1,800 years ago, a Roman household in what is now Turkey decorated the floor of its home with a detailed mosaic showing animals and mythological figures. Among them were a cat and a dog whose names were written beside their images. Archaeologists have now uncovered the mosaic at the ancient city of Adramytteion on Turkey’s Aegean coast.The colourful floor was part of a Roman villa dating to the late second to third centuries AD, according to Live Science report. The residence had three halls arranged around a central atrium, along with several smaller rooms and a network of pipes and drains that may have been connected to a latrine. One of the halls appears to have been used as the main reception area of the villa.It was here that archaeologists found the large mosaic. The floor decoration measures about 16.4 by 11.8 feet (5 by 3.6 metres) and is divided into 15 separate panels arranged in three rows. Most of the panels show animals, including birds, fish and felines. Two others feature mythological figures- a gorgon, possibly Medusa, and a winged horse, possibly Pegasus.The mosaic was made using tiles in several colours, including white, black, red, orange, yellow, pink, burgundy, blue, turquoise and green. But among all these images, two animals stand out because their names were included in the artwork. One is a light-coloured cat called Emerald. The other is a dog named Ocean.Emerald The Cat Was Shown Resting On A CushionThe panel showing Emerald was positioned on the left side of the room as a visitor entered. It depicts a pale-coloured cat sitting on a blue-green cushion. Above the animal are Greek letters spelling “Zmaragdin”, meaning emerald.The way the cat is shown has helped archaeologists consider what its role may have been in the household. Emerald is sitting calmly on a cushion rather than being shown as a wild or stray animal. This suggests that the cat may have been a pet.Archaeologist Hüseyin Özgen, head of the Adramytteion research team at Mimar Sinan Fine Arts University, wrote about the mosaic in a study that is forthcoming in the Journal of Mosaic Research. He noted that Emerald and Ocean may preserve the memory of animals familiar to the people who lived in the villa.There is also a possible explanation for why the cat was given the name Emerald. Özgen suggested that the name could be connected to Roman Egypt, where emeralds were mined in antiquity. The villa’s owner may have had trading connections with North Africa, although this remains a possible explanation for the name.Ocean The Dog Was Named In GreekOn the right side of the room, another panel shows a dog running or leaping. The animal is labelled with the Greek letters “Okeanos”, meaning ocean.The name may have had a connection with the location where the villa stood. Adramytteion was a harbour city, and Özgen suggested that the dog may have been given the name Ocean because of its surroundings.Unlike the other animals in the mosaic, Emerald and Ocean are specifically named. This makes their panels particularly interesting to archaeologists because the names could provide a small glimpse into the lives of the people who used the villa.The two animals may have been pets, but the evidence does not establish this with certainty. Özgen wrote that Emerald and Ocean were likely familiar to the villa’s residents, even if they were not specifically household pets. Their images may have also served as familiar signs of ownership and household identity.Villa Was Excavated RecentlyThe discovery is part of ongoing archaeological work at Adramytteion. Özgen began excavations at the ancient site in 2012, but the Roman villa was discovered only recently. Archaeologists excavated the residence in 2025 and early 2026.During the Roman period, Adramytteion was a provincial capital in Asia Minor. Its position at the head of a gulf on the Aegean Sea also made it an important trading location.The villa appears to have been an impressive residence. It included three halls with mosaic floors, several secondary rooms and the system of pipes and drains. According to Özgen, visitors approaching the residence from its courtyard would have entered towards the largest and most elaborate mosaic in the home.Research at Adramytteion is continuing. The findings on the mosaic are included in Hüseyin M. Özgen’s 2026 study, Mosaic Programmes and Architectural Transformation in an Atrium-Centred Roman-Period Residence at Adramytteion: The North, East and South Halls, forthcoming in the Journal of Mosaic Research.

articles.title: Google’s revived nuclear power plant gets $1.9B loan from US government | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Google said it would bring an Iowa nuclear power plant back from the dead. Now, the plant's owner is getting a $1.9B loan from the U.S. Energy Department.
articles.body:
Last October, Google said it would bring an Iowa nuclear power plant back from the dead . Now, the facility’s owner, NextEra Energy, has received a $1.9 billion loan from the U.S. Department of Energy to finance the refurbishment.

The sizable loan is the second of its kind, suggesting that the Trump administration views revived nuclear power as a key source of electricity for tech companies seeking to power their AI data centers. Last year, the Department of Energy extended a $1 billion loan to Constellation Energy to restart a reactor at Three Mile Island.

James Danly, Deputy Secretary of Energy, said that the Iowa power plant’s restart in 2029 will “drive down electricity costs,” though he did not explain how. Just 50 megawatts will be set aside for the local power cooperative, NextEra CEO John Ketchum said during an earnings call last year. That capacity would cover 18% of Iowa’s demand growth since 2021, the year before ChatGPT was released.

Google is reportedly looking to build up to six data centers near the Duane Arnold Energy Center, which hasn’t operated since 2020 when an intense rainstorm damaged the power plant. Rather than repair it, NextEra decided to mothball it. At the time, cheap natural gas was flooding the market, making nuclear power economically unappealing .

A lot has changed in the last six years, though. After decades of little growth in demand, the sudden rise of AI coupled with broader electrification of the economy meant that utilities and power providers were suddenly scrambling to find new generating sources of electricity. New data centers are expected to nearly triple the sector’s electricity demand by 2035.

Shuttered nuclear power plants are becoming one of the tech industry’s favorite choices to quickly provide clean, firm power.

Microsoft signed a deal with Constellation Energy two years ago to restart a reactor at Three Mile Island that last operated in 2019. The reactor is scheduled to restart in 2028 and generate 835 megawatts.

Another facility in Illinois, Constellation Energy’s Clinton Clean Energy Center, was in danger of closing down before its parent found a new customer in Meta , which is buying all of the clean energy attributes from the 1.1 gigawatt power plant. The arrangement will see Clinton sending its electrons to the local grid, while Meta will use the certificates to offset emissions it is producing elsewhere. The tech giant’s Hyperion AI data center, for example, will need 10 natural gas power plants to operate. If completed, the data center will consume more electricity than all of South Dakota .

Duane Arnold is smaller, but in the process of refurbishment, NextEra will squeeze an additional 14 megawatts from the facility, bringing the total to 615 megawatts.

Altogether, the three power plants represent the lowest hanging fruit in the U.S. There might be one or two more, according to a report from UtilityDive, though those candidates, including San Onofre in California, have been shuttered for longer and would require more work to bring back online.
